75.sec: Capital flight and external vulnerability  [other exams]

75.s: The special FCNR(B) deposit scheme in July 2026 was described as a ‘one-time comfort’ because it:
o: Converted all foreign portfolio investment into foreign direct investment
Eliminated India’s merchandise deficit permanently through higher exports
Reduced India’s external debt to zero
Drew $127 billion in NRI deposits and temporarily supported the capital account and overall BoP surplus
75.x: The scheme drew $127 billion in NRI deposits, contributing to a $27.7 billion capital-account surplus and a $20.8 billion overall BoP surplus. Its support was viewed as temporary or one-time.
75.tq: Link a policy instrument to its immediate balance-of-payments effect without inferring a permanent structural change.
75.sec: Capital flight and external vulnerability  [other exams]

75.s:
Which of the following are safeguards against external vulnerability?
1. Maintaining adequate foreign-exchange reserves sufficient for import cover
2. Keeping short-term external debt low
3. Reducing reliance on volatile FPI and debt flows
4. Increasing dependence on hot money
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
75.x: Adequate reserves, low short-term debt and reduced dependence on volatile FPI and debt flows strengthen external resilience. Greater dependence on hot money increases vulnerability.
75.tq: Identify the protective measures and reject the deliberately reversed safeguard.
75.sec: Capital flight and external vulnerability  [other exams]

75.s: How do increases in US Federal Reserve interest rates and a strong US dollar generally affect emerging markets such as India?
o: They automatically increase India’s net FDI
They raise US yields, attract hot money away from emerging markets and weaken the rupee
They reduce US yields and cause capital to flow into emerging markets
They eliminate exchange-rate volatility in emerging markets
75.x: US rate hikes and a strong dollar raise US yields, encouraging hot-money outflows from emerging markets and putting downward pressure on the rupee.
75.tq: Follow the capital-flow chain from interest-rate differential to exchange-rate pressure.
75.sec: Capital flight and external vulnerability  [other exams]

75.s: During the 2013 taper tantrum, Morgan Stanley included India among the:
75.x: Morgan Stanley described India as one of the ‘Fragile Five’ during the 2013 taper tantrum because of external-sector vulnerability.
75.tq: Recall the distinctive group label associated with the external shock.
75.sec: Capital flight and external vulnerability  [other exams]

75.s: Which one of the following combinations is correctly matched with weak net capital flows?
o: Lower outward FDI, higher portfolio inflows and reduced private-equity exits; outward FDI rose 75 per cent to $127 billion
IPO exits by PE/VC, rising FPI purchases and lower US tariffs; outward FDI fell to $7.6 billion
Higher remittances, stronger FPI inflows and US tariff cuts; outward FDI rose to $44.0 billion
IPO exits by PE/VC, FPI sell-offs and US tariffs; outward FDI rose 75 per cent to $29.2 billion
75.x: Weak net capital was associated with PE/VC IPO exits, FPI sell-offs and US tariffs. Outward FDI rose by 75 per cent to $29.2 billion.
75.tq: Use the correctly matched cluster of causes and the associated outward-FDI figure.
75.sec: Capital flight and external vulnerability  [other exams]

75.s: In January 2026, India’s foreign-exchange reserves of $701.4 billion covered approximately what proportion of external debt?
75.x: Foreign-exchange reserves of $701.4 billion in January 2026 covered about 94 per cent of India’s external debt.
75.tq: Associate the reserve figure with its stated coverage ratio rather than treating reserves as exceeding debt.
75.sec: Capital flight and external vulnerability  [other exams]

75.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes current account convertibility from capital account convertibility?
o: Capital account convertibility covers remittances only, while current account convertibility covers government borrowing
Current account convertibility covers trade, income and transfers, while capital account convertibility covers FDI, portfolio investment and borrowing
Current account convertibility concerns FDI, while capital account convertibility concerns only merchandise trade
Both forms of convertibility concern only official foreign-exchange reserves
75.x: Current account convertibility permits free conversion for trade, income and transfers. Capital account convertibility relates to FDI, portfolio investment and borrowing.
75.tq: Separate routine international transactions from transactions involving assets and liabilities.
75.sec: Convertibility - current vs capital, year, committees  [other exams]

75.s:
Arrange the following developments relating to exchange-rate reform in India in chronological order:
A. Unified exchange rate introduced
B. LERMS introduced
C. Full current account convertibility accepted through Article VIII of the IMF
D. Second Tarapore Committee set up
75.x: LERMS was introduced in 1992-93, the unified rate was introduced on 1 March 1993, full current account convertibility followed in August 1994, and the second Tarapore Committee was set up in 2006.
75.tq: Fix the sequence using the dated milestones before placing the later committee.
75.sec: Convertibility - current vs capital, year, committees  [other exams]

75.s: Under the Liberalised Exchange Rate Management System (LERMS), the exchange rate was determined through which arrangement?
o: 60 per cent official rate and 40 per cent market rate
40 per cent official rate and 60 per cent market rate
100 per cent market rate from the beginning
75.x: LERMS, introduced in the 1992-93 Budget, used a dual exchange-rate system comprising 40 per cent official rate and 60 per cent market rate.
75.tq: Remember the direction of the two percentages instead of reversing the official and market shares.
75.sec: Convertibility - current vs capital, year, committees  [other exams]

75.s: India achieved full current account convertibility in August 1994 by:
o: Setting up the second Tarapore Committee
Accepting Article VIII of the IMF
75.x: Full current account convertibility was achieved in August 1994 when India accepted the obligations under Article VIII of the IMF.
75.tq: Match the convertibility milestone with the specific IMF provision rather than with a domestic statute.
75.sec: Convertibility - current vs capital, year, committees  [other exams]

75.s: The second committee on capital account convertibility was set up by the Reserve Bank of India on:
75.x: The RBI set up the second Tarapore Committee on 31 July 2006.
75.tq: Use the exact committee-constitution date and distinguish it from the dates of FEMA and exchange-rate reforms.
75.sec: Convertibility - current vs capital, year, committees  [other exams]

75.s: India delinked the rupee from sterling in:
75.x: The Indian rupee was delinked from sterling in September 1975.
75.tq: Recall the historical exchange-rate milestone independently of the later convertibility reforms.
75.sec: Convertibility - current vs capital, year, committees  [other exams]

75.s: India was estimated to be the world's largest recipient of remittances in FY25. What was the approximate amount of remittances and their share in India's GDP, respectively?
75.x: India received approximately $135.4 billion in remittances in FY25, equivalent to about 3.5% of its GDP.
75.tq: Use the paired numerical figures and distinguish the annual estimate from other remittance measures.
75.sec: Remittances - rank and sources

75.s: Which one of the following is the correct order of the leading sources of remittances to India, beginning with the largest source?
o: Singapore, United Kingdom, United Arab Emirates, United States
United States, United Arab Emirates, United Kingdom, Singapore
United Arab Emirates, United States, Singapore, United Kingdom
United States, United Kingdom, United Arab Emirates, Singapore
75.x: The United States is the largest source of remittances to India, accounting for 27.7%, followed by the UAE, the UK and Singapore.
75.tq: Test the exact order in a ranked list rather than relying on general regional associations.
75.sec: Remittances - rank and sources

75.s:
Consider the following statements regarding India's remittances:
1. Workers' remittances reached $110.47 billion in FY26, compared with $87.55 billion earlier.
2. Remittances received in the fourth quarter of FY26 amounted to $31.07 billion.
3. The fourth-quarter figure represented a 13-year high.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
75.x: All three statements are correct. The FY26 workers' remittance figure was $110.47 billion, while Q4 FY26 remittances were $31.07 billion, a 13-year high.
75.tq: Check all three related numerical statements before selecting the combined option.
75.sec: Remittances - rank and sources

75.s: Which one of the following best explains the significance of remittances in India's external sector?
o: They are counter-cyclical and do not create a debt burden or repayment obligation.
They are classified entirely as foreign direct investment inflows.
They can be received only through external commercial borrowings.
They are pro-cyclical and create a direct repayment obligation for the recipient country.
75.x: Remittances are counter-cyclical and do not create a repayment obligation, unlike debt-related flows such as ECBs or certain portfolio liabilities.
75.tq: Apply the contrast between stable transfer inflows and debt-creating capital flows.
75.sec: Remittances - rank and sources

75.s:
With reference to invisibles in the balance of payments, consider the following statements:
1. Invisibles include services, primary income and transfers.
2. Non-factor services include shipping, banking, tourism and software.
3. Factor income is distinct from non-factor services.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
75.x: Invisibles comprise services, primary income and transfers. Services include non-factor activities such as shipping, banking, tourism and software, while factor income is separately identified.
75.tq: Group the components of invisibles and distinguish factor from non-factor services.
75.sec: Remittances - rank and sources

75.s: Which one of the following correctly describes India's net primary income in the first quarter of FY27?
o: It was an outflow of $10.5 billion.
It was an outflow of $135.4 billion.
It was an inflow of $10.5 billion.
It was an inflow of $31.07 billion.
75.x: India's net primary income was an outflow of $10.5 billion in Q1 FY27.
75.tq: Discriminate between an income inflow and an income outflow while retaining the exact figure.
75.sec: Remittances - rank and sources

75.s:
A country records a current account deficit. Which of the following can finance that deficit?
1. A surplus in the capital account through net capital inflows
2. Drawing down foreign exchange reserves
3. The monetary authority acting as the ultimate financier of a balance of payments deficit
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
75.x: A CAD may be financed through capital-account inflows or by using reserves. More generally, the monetary authority is the ultimate financier of a balance of payments deficit.
75.tq: Test the financing routes of a deficit by separating external inflows from reserve use.
75.sec: Accounting identity - BoP vs balance of trade, errors and omissions, reserves

75.s: Which one of the following statements correctly distinguishes Balance of Trade from Balance of Payments?
o: Balance of Trade is always equal to the current account balance.
Balance of Trade covers merchandise exports and imports only, whereas Balance of Payments records the complete set of external transactions.
Balance of Trade includes all capital and financial transactions, whereas Balance of Payments includes only merchandise trade.
Balance of Payments excludes services and transfers because they are invisible items.
75.x: Balance of Trade equals merchandise exports minus merchandise imports and is a part of the current account. Balance of Payments is the broader record of external transactions.
75.tq: Split the narrower merchandise measure from the comprehensive external-account measure.
75.sec: Accounting identity - BoP vs balance of trade, errors and omissions, reserves

75.s:
Consider the following statements about transactions in the balance of payments:
1. Autonomous transactions take place for their own sake.
2. Accommodating transactions are undertaken to fill the gap arising from other transactions.
3. Reserve changes and official borrowing are examples of accommodating transactions.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
75.x: Autonomous transactions are motivated by their own economic purpose. Accommodating transactions, including reserve changes and official borrowing, help finance or fill the resulting gap.
75.tq: Distinguish transactions by their purpose rather than by the account in which they appear.
75.sec: Accounting identity - BoP vs balance of trade, errors and omissions, reserves

75.s: What is the usual effect of the overall balance of payments position on foreign exchange reserves?
o: The overall balance has no relationship with reserve movements.
A positive overall balance reduces reserves, while a negative balance increases them.
A positive overall balance adds to reserves, while a negative balance draws them down.
Both positive and negative balances increase reserves because the BoP always balances in accounting terms.
75.x: A positive overall balance adds to foreign exchange reserves, whereas a negative overall balance draws them down. If reserves become insufficient, a balance of payments crisis may result.
75.tq: Use the direction of reserve movement to identify the correct surplus-deficit relationship.
75.sec: Accounting identity - BoP vs balance of trade, errors and omissions, reserves

75.s: The primary purpose of IMF finance in relation to a country's external sector is to
o: correct disequilibrium in the balance of payments, especially in a crisis.
finance permanent infrastructure expenditure without conditions.
provide grants for increasing merchandise exports.
determine the country's exchange rate independently of its monetary authority.
75.x: IMF finance is generally treated as a last resort for correcting balance of payments disequilibrium, particularly during an external crisis.
75.tq: Identify the institution by matching its principal function with the external-sector problem.
75.sec: IMF role - BoP support facilities, SDR

75.s:
Which of the following are principal IMF lending windows used for balance of payments support?
1. Stand-By Arrangement
2. Extended Fund Facility
3. Foreign Currency Swap Facility of the Reserve Bank of India
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
75.x: Stand-By Arrangement and Extended Fund Facility are IMF balance of payments lending windows. The Foreign Currency Swap Facility of the RBI is not an IMF lending window.
75.tq: Eliminate the institutionally mismatched facility by asking which body operates it.
75.sec: IMF role - BoP support facilities, SDR

75.s: India drew on IMF assistance during which of the following situations?
o: The balance of payments crisis of 1991
The remittance inflow surge of FY26
75.x: India obtained IMF assistance during the severe balance of payments crisis of 1991.
75.tq: Link the international institution to the specific crisis year rather than to later external-sector developments.
75.sec: IMF role - BoP support facilities, SDR

75.s: The High Level Committee on Balance of Payments headed by C. Rangarajan during 1991–93 regarded a sustainable current account deficit as approximately
75.x: The C. Rangarajan Committee placed a sustainable CAD at approximately 1.6% of GDP and also recommended a market-determined exchange rate.
75.tq: Retain the committee-specific threshold and distinguish it from contemporary CAD figures.
75.sec: Sustainable CAD threshold (Rangarajan committee)

75.s: Which additional recommendation was associated with the High Level Committee on Balance of Payments headed by C. Rangarajan?
o: A permanently fixed exchange rate determined by the IMF
Replacement of the current account by the capital account
75.x: Along with identifying a sustainable CAD of about 1.6% of GDP, the committee recommended a market-determined exchange rate.
75.tq: Pair the committee with its specific policy recommendation rather than its numerical threshold alone.
75.sec: Sustainable CAD threshold (Rangarajan committee)

75.s: India's current account position in June 2026 was characterised by which of the following?
o: A deficit of $6.2 billion against a merchandise gap of $30.2 billion
A surplus of $1.2 billion against a merchandise gap of $6.2 billion
A surplus of $6.2 billion against a merchandise gap of $30.2 billion
A deficit of $30.2 billion against a merchandise surplus of $6.2 billion
75.x: The CAD widened to $6.2 billion in June 2026, from a surplus of $1.2 billion a year earlier, amid a merchandise gap of $30.2 billion.
75.tq: Match the deficit, comparison-year surplus and merchandise gap without reversing their signs.
75.sec: Universal angles

75.s:
Consider the following statements regarding India's external-sector position in H1 FY26:
1. India's CAD was 0.8% of GDP.
2. This CAD was lower than the corresponding high-deficit positions of Brazil, Australia and the United Kingdom.
3. The rupee fell by approximately 6.5% against the US dollar.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
75.x: All three statements are correct: the H1 FY26 CAD was 0.8% of GDP, lower than the cited high-deficit peers, while the rupee depreciated by about 6.5% against the dollar.
75.tq: Combine the percentage, peer comparison and exchange-rate movement before choosing the coded answer.
75.sec: Universal angles

75.s: Why are FCNR(B) deposits and external commercial borrowings viewed cautiously in discussions on India's external-sector sustainability?
o: They are domestic tax receipts and do not affect the balance of payments.
They are temporary inflows, whereas FDI is expected to support a self-sustaining capital surplus.
They are permanent grants and therefore cannot reverse suddenly.
They are components of merchandise exports and reduce the trade deficit directly.
75.x: FCNR(B) and ECB inflows are considered temporary sources of financing. The preferred long-term basis for a self-sustaining capital surplus is stronger FDI.
75.tq: Distinguish temporary financing flows from durable investment flows.
75.sec: Universal angles

75.s: Which one of the following correctly describes India's external-sector position in Q1 FY27 and July 2026?
o: CAD was 6.2% of GDP, and FCNR(B) inflows had no effect on the balance of payments.
There was a current account surplus of 0.5% of GDP, caused entirely by merchandise exports.
CAD was 1.6% of GDP, and FCNR(B) inflows produced a balance of payments deficit in July 2026.
CAD was 0.5% of GDP, and FCNR(B) inflows contributed to a balance of payments surplus in July 2026.
75.x: The CAD was 0.5% of GDP in Q1 FY27, while FCNR(B) inflows helped produce a balance of payments surplus in July 2026.
75.tq: Keep the two time references separate and match each with its correct external-sector outcome.
75.sec: Universal angles

75.s: India ran a current account surplus for three consecutive years only during which period?
75.x: India recorded a current account surplus for three straight years only during 2000–03.
75.tq: Use the distinctive first-and-last period clue to identify the correct sequence of years.
75.sec: Universal angles

75.s: Which one of the following reflects a criticism of excessive reliance on remittances and one-time deposit schemes?
o: They are always more volatile than merchandise imports because they are recorded as trade flows.
They may substitute for stable foreign direct investment and do not by themselves ensure long-term external-sector sustainability.
They eliminate the need for foreign exchange reserves.
They necessarily create a stable and self-sustaining capital surplus irrespective of their duration.
75.x: Dependence on remittances and one-time deposit schemes may provide useful financing but does not replace stable FDI or guarantee a self-sustaining capital surplus.
75.tq: Apply the sustainability test by comparing recurring investment with temporary or transfer-based financing.
75.sec: Universal angles

76.s: Under which exchange-rate regime does depreciation occur as a result of market demand and supply?
76.x: Depreciation is a market-determined fall in the value of a currency under a flexible or floating exchange-rate regime.
76.tq: Identify the regime before distinguishing market-driven and officially ordered changes.
76.sec: Devaluation vs depreciation, appreciation vs revaluation - meaning and trade effects  [APPSC]

76.s:
With reference to exchange-rate terminology, consider the following statements:
1. Depreciation under a floating regime means that more units of domestic currency are required per unit of foreign currency.
2. Appreciation under a floating regime means that fewer units of domestic currency are required per unit of foreign currency.
3. Both depreciation and appreciation are officially ordered changes under a fixed exchange-rate regime.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
76.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because depreciation and appreciation are market-driven changes under a flexible regime; official changes under a fixed regime are devaluation and revaluation.
76.tq: Separate the market-driven pair from the authority-driven pair.
76.sec: Devaluation vs depreciation, appreciation vs revaluation - meaning and trade effects  [APPSC]

76.s: Which one of the following correctly describes devaluation?
o: A temporary increase in the demand for a foreign currency
A market-driven rise in the value of a currency under a floating regime
An official lowering of a currency's value against a reference currency or basket under a fixed regime
An official rise in a currency's value under a floating regime
76.x: Devaluation is an official reduction in the value of a currency against a reference currency or basket under a fixed exchange-rate regime.
76.tq: Ask who takes the action and under which regime.
76.sec: Devaluation vs depreciation, appreciation vs revaluation - meaning and trade effects  [APPSC]

76.s:
Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?

1. Devaluation — Official raising of the currency's value under a fixed regime
2. Revaluation — Official raising of the currency's value under a fixed regime
3. Depreciation — Market raising of the domestic-currency price of foreign currency
4. Appreciation — Market lowering of the domestic-currency price of foreign currency
76.x: Devaluation lowers the currency's official value, whereas revaluation raises it. Depreciation raises and appreciation lowers the domestic-currency price of foreign currency in a floating regime.
76.tq: Use the official-versus-market distinction to eliminate reversed definitions.
76.sec: Devaluation vs depreciation, appreciation vs revaluation - meaning and trade effects  [APPSC]

76.s: If the exchange rate changes from ₹94 per dollar to ₹96 per dollar, which of the following is the correct inference?
o: The dollar has depreciated against the rupee
The rupee has been officially revalued
76.x: A rise in the number of rupees required to buy one dollar indicates depreciation of the rupee. The information does not by itself establish an official revaluation or devaluation.
76.tq: Read a direct quote by checking whether more or fewer rupees buy one dollar.
76.sec: Devaluation vs depreciation, appreciation vs revaluation - meaning and trade effects  [APPSC]

76.s: Devaluation is described as an expenditure-switching policy because it generally:
o: Raises export prices in foreign currency and lowers import prices
Makes imports cheaper and encourages spending on foreign goods
Makes domestic goods cheaper for foreigners and imports costlier for domestic consumers
Eliminates the need for fiscal and monetary measures
76.x: Devaluation makes home-produced goods relatively cheaper for foreigners and imported goods costlier at home, thereby switching expenditure towards domestic production.
76.tq: Apply the price effects of a weaker currency to domestic and foreign spending.
76.sec: Devaluation vs depreciation, appreciation vs revaluation - meaning and trade effects  [APPSC]

76.s:
Consider the following statements regarding devaluation or depreciation:
1. They tend to make exports cheaper in foreign-currency terms.
2. They tend to make imports dearer in domestic-currency terms.
3. They necessarily raise the foreign-currency prices of exports.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
76.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct and generally improve the trade balance. Statement 3 is false because exports become cheaper, not costlier, in foreign-currency terms.
76.tq: Spot the reversed trade-price effect in the false statement.
76.sec: Devaluation vs depreciation, appreciation vs revaluation - meaning and trade effects  [APPSC]

76.s:
Assertion (A): Devaluation tends to improve the balance of trade.
Reason (R): Devaluation raises the foreign-currency prices of exports.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
76.x: Devaluation tends to improve the balance of trade because exports become cheaper abroad and imports become costlier at home. The reason is false because devaluation lowers, rather than raises, export prices in foreign-currency terms.
76.tq: Test whether the reason reverses the direction of the price effect.
76.sec: Devaluation vs depreciation, appreciation vs revaluation - meaning and trade effects  [APPSC]

76.s:
Which of the following can limit the improvement in the trade balance following depreciation of the domestic currency?

1. Imported inflation
2. Inelastic demand for oil
3. Costlier repayment of external commercial borrowings

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
76.x: Depreciation can generate imported inflation, increase the domestic cost of oil when demand is inelastic, and make repayment of foreign-currency external commercial borrowings costlier.
76.tq: Group all the stated adverse consequences before selecting the complete combination.
76.sec: Devaluation vs depreciation, appreciation vs revaluation - meaning and trade effects  [APPSC]

76.s: Why can a falling rupee widen India's current account deficit when oil demand is inelastic?
o: Because depreciation automatically stops oil imports
Because export prices rise in foreign currency
Because a weaker rupee lowers the domestic price of imported oil
Because inelastic oil demand prevents a sufficient reduction in import quantity despite the higher rupee cost
76.x: When oil demand is inelastic, depreciation raises the rupee cost of oil without causing a proportionate fall in quantity imported, which can widen the current account deficit.
76.tq: Link exchange-rate movement with import demand elasticity.
76.sec: Devaluation vs depreciation, appreciation vs revaluation - meaning and trade effects  [APPSC]

76.s: According to the Economic Survey 2025-26 assessment stated for exchange-rate effects, a weaker rupee has what net effect?
o: It benefits only the financial channel and worsens the trade balance
It helps India's trade balance more than it hurts through capital outflows
It hurts the trade balance more than the financial channel benefits it
It has no effect on either trade or capital flows
76.x: The Economic Survey 2025-26 assessment is that the trade-balance benefit of a weaker currency exceeds the adverse effect through capital outflows.
76.tq: Distinguish the net assessment from one isolated adverse channel.
76.sec: Devaluation vs depreciation, appreciation vs revaluation - meaning and trade effects  [APPSC]

76.s: Which one of the following statements regarding the rupee movement mentioned for FY 2025-26 is correct?
o: The rupee remained unchanged against the yen up to January 2026
The rupee depreciated by 6.3% during the whole of FY 2025-26
The rupee depreciated by 5.4% up to January 2026 and was among the currencies most depreciated along with the yen
The rupee appreciated by 5.4% up to January 2026
76.x: The rupee recorded a 5.4% depreciation in FY 2025-26 up to January and was among the most depreciated currencies, along with the yen.
76.tq: Check both the direction and the stated percentage before choosing the option.
76.sec: Devaluation vs depreciation, appreciation vs revaluation - meaning and trade effects  [APPSC]

76.s: India's last formal devaluation of the rupee was undertaken:
o: In a single step in July 1991
In a single step in January 1992
76.x: India's last formal devaluation was a two-step exercise undertaken in July 1991.
76.tq: Use the number of steps and the date together to reject near-date distractors.
76.sec: Devaluation vs depreciation, appreciation vs revaluation - meaning and trade effects  [APPSC]

76.s: A direct exchange-rate quotation expresses:
o: The annual percentage change in the exchange rate
Units of foreign currency per one unit of domestic currency
The number of months of import cover
Units of domestic currency per one unit of foreign currency
76.x: A direct quote states the amount of domestic currency required for one unit of foreign currency, such as ₹95 = $1.
76.tq: Identify the domestic-currency side of the quotation.
76.sec: Exchange rate terms - direct/indirect quote, NEER, REER, spot, forward, arbitrage, hot currency  [APPSC]

76.s: Which of the following represents an indirect quotation from the perspective of India?
76.x: An indirect quote expresses units of foreign currency per unit of domestic currency. Thus, $0.0105 per ₹1 is an indirect quotation for India.
76.tq: Reverse the direct quote carefully and identify foreign currency per rupee.
76.sec: Exchange rate terms - direct/indirect quote, NEER, REER, spot, forward, arbitrage, hot currency  [APPSC]

76.s: The Nominal Effective Exchange Rate (NEER) of the rupee is best described as:
o: The number of months for which reserves can finance imports
The rupee's exchange rate against the US dollar alone
A weighted average of the rupee against the currencies of major trading partners
The exchange rate adjusted only for domestic inflation
76.x: NEER is a weighted average of the rupee against a basket of currencies of major trading partners. Its stated base is 2015-16 = 100.
76.tq: Distinguish a trade-weighted index from a bilateral exchange rate.
76.sec: Exchange rate terms - direct/indirect quote, NEER, REER, spot, forward, arbitrage, hot currency  [APPSC]

76.s: The base year specified for India's NEER in the given exchange-rate framework is:
76.x: The NEER series referred to has 2015-16 as its base, assigned the value 100.
76.tq: Recall the index base rather than confusing it with a general inflation base year.
76.sec: Exchange rate terms - direct/indirect quote, NEER, REER, spot, forward, arbitrage, hot currency  [APPSC]

76.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. A rise in NEER indicates appreciation of the rupee.
2. REER adjusts NEER for inflation differentials.
3. REER is calculated as NEER × (domestic prices / foreign prices).
Which of the statements given above are correct?
76.x: All three statements are correct. REER incorporates relative price levels through the stated formula, while a rising NEER indicates nominal appreciation of the rupee.
76.tq: Combine the definition, direction of movement and formula before selecting the complete code.
76.sec: Exchange rate terms - direct/indirect quote, NEER, REER, spot, forward, arbitrage, hot currency  [APPSC]

76.s: Which one of the following statements about REER is NOT correct?
o: It is a less useful indicator of competitiveness than an unadjusted bilateral exchange rate
A high REER may indicate that the currency is overvalued
It incorporates inflation differentials between domestic and foreign economies
A low REER may indicate that the currency is undervalued
76.x: REER is regarded as the better indicator of competitiveness because it adjusts the nominal effective exchange rate for inflation differentials. The other statements correctly describe REER.
76.tq: Find the option that reverses the comparative usefulness of REER.
76.sec: Exchange rate terms - direct/indirect quote, NEER, REER, spot, forward, arbitrage, hot currency  [APPSC]

76.s: Which of the following correctly distinguishes spot and forward exchange rates?
o: A spot rate is for immediate delivery, whereas a forward rate is agreed now for delivery on a future date
A forward rate is determined only after the future delivery date
A spot rate is agreed today for future delivery, whereas a forward rate is for immediate delivery
Both rates necessarily relate only to cash transactions settled on the same day
76.x: A spot rate applies to immediate delivery, while a forward rate is fixed by agreement today for settlement at a specified future date.
76.tq: Use the timing of delivery to separate two closely related terms.
76.sec: Exchange rate terms - direct/indirect quote, NEER, REER, spot, forward, arbitrage, hot currency  [APPSC]

76.s: Settlement under a spot foreign-exchange transaction generally takes place:
o: Only at the end of the financial year
76.x: A spot transaction generally involves settlement within two days. A forward transaction fixes the rate today for a future date.
76.tq: Use the settlement period to distinguish spot from forward transactions.
76.sec: Exchange rate terms - direct/indirect quote, NEER, REER, spot, forward, arbitrage, hot currency  [APPSC]

76.s: An importer enters into a forward contract primarily for which purpose?
o: To increase the country's import cover automatically
To cover exchange-rate risk by fixing a rate for a future transaction
To convert a floating exchange-rate regime into a fixed regime
To obtain an official revaluation from the monetary authority
76.x: Hedging involves covering exchange-rate risk, and a forward contract can fix the exchange rate today for a transaction to be settled in the future.
76.tq: Apply the risk-management purpose of a forward contract to a trade transaction.
76.sec: Exchange rate terms - direct/indirect quote, NEER, REER, spot, forward, arbitrage, hot currency  [APPSC]

76.s: Which of the following statements about an exchange-rate regime is correct?
o: It is the system by which a country manages its currency
It refers only to the country's foreign-exchange reserves
It is limited to the method of calculating REER
It refers exclusively to the official exchange rate under a fixed system
76.x: An exchange-rate regime is the system through which a country manages its currency. The two broad types are fixed and floating regimes.
76.tq: Select the broad definition instead of a component or subtype.
76.sec: Exchange rate terms - direct/indirect quote, NEER, REER, spot, forward, arbitrage, hot currency  [APPSC]

76.s: In foreign-exchange terminology, a 'hot currency' refers to:
o: A currency temporarily attracting strong demand as a hard currency in the forex market
A currency that is easily available and therefore called soft
A currency whose value is fixed permanently by the central bank
A currency used only for settlement of oil imports
76.x: Hot currency is a temporary term for a hard currency attracting strong confidence or demand in the foreign-exchange market. A soft currency is generally easily available and less strongly valued.
76.tq: Distinguish the temporary market label from the formal hard-versus-soft classification.
76.sec: Exchange rate terms - direct/indirect quote, NEER, REER, spot, forward, arbitrage, hot currency  [APPSC]

76.s: Which one of the following correctly describes import cover?
o: The number of months for which a country's reserves can pay for its imports
The share of imports financed by foreign direct investment
The period during which a forward exchange contract remains valid
The percentage change in the exchange rate during a year
76.x: Import cover measures the number of months for which available foreign-exchange reserves can finance imports.
76.tq: Match the term with the unit in which it is conventionally expressed.
76.sec: Exchange rate terms - direct/indirect quote, NEER, REER, spot, forward, arbitrage, hot currency  [APPSC]

76.s: Which of the following is a correct grouping of participants in the foreign-exchange market?
o: Commercial banks, authorised dealers or brokers, and monetary authorities
Only monetary authorities and stock exchanges
Exporters, courts and local governments exclusively
76.x: The principal participants identified are commercial banks, authorised dealers or brokers, and monetary authorities.
76.tq: Choose the complete institutional group rather than an incomplete or exaggerated grouping.
76.sec: Exchange rate terms - direct/indirect quote, NEER, REER, spot, forward, arbitrage, hot currency  [APPSC]

76.s:
Arrange the following exchange-rate concepts from the least adjusted measure to the most inflation-adjusted measure:
A. Bilateral nominal exchange rate
B. NEER
C. REER

Select the correct sequence.
76.x: A bilateral nominal rate concerns two currencies, NEER aggregates nominal rates against a trade-weighted basket, and REER further adjusts NEER for inflation differentials.
76.tq: Build the sequence by adding the successive layers of aggregation and inflation adjustment.
76.sec: Exchange rate terms - direct/indirect quote, NEER, REER, spot, forward, arbitrage, hot currency  [APPSC]

76.s: Which of the following is a conventional market intervention measure used by the Reserve Bank of India to moderate excessive rupee volatility?
o: Fixing the fiscal deficit at a statutory percentage
Selling dollars from its foreign exchange reserves
Increasing customs duties on all imports
76.x: The RBI may sell dollars from its foreign exchange reserves as a spot intervention to moderate excessive volatility in the rupee.
76.tq: Identify the institution that directly operates in the foreign exchange market.
76.sec: RBI tools to manage rupee volatility and stop a slide

76.s: Which one of the following is NOT a tool of the Reserve Bank of India for managing rupee volatility?
76.x: Fiscal policy adjustments are Government measures, not RBI exchange-rate management tools. Spot intervention, forex swaps and monetary policy signalling are RBI tools.
76.tq: Find the institutionally misplaced policy instrument.
76.sec: RBI tools to manage rupee volatility and stop a slide

76.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the objective of RBI intervention in the foreign exchange market:
1. It primarily aims to curb excessive volatility.
2. It necessarily aims to defend one permanently fixed rupee-dollar level.
3. It may use foreign exchange reserves for intervention.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
76.x: The RBI intervenes mainly to curb volatility, not to defend a permanently fixed exchange-rate level. Use of reserves is one possible intervention method.
76.tq: Separate the stated objective from an extreme claim about permanently fixing the exchange rate.
76.sec: RBI tools to manage rupee volatility and stop a slide

76.s: In the context of offshore Non-Deliverable Forward markets, which measure is used by the RBI to reduce speculative pressure on the rupee?
o: Abolishing all forward contracts in India
Restricting domestic banks’ participation in offshore NDF markets and enforcing Net Open Position limits
Permitting unlimited offshore positions by domestic banks
76.x: The RBI restricts domestic banks’ offshore NDF participation and enforces Net Open Position limits to curb speculative pressure and volatility.
76.tq: Match the regulatory action with the market through which pressure is transmitted.
76.sec: RBI tools to manage rupee volatility and stop a slide

76.s: The Non-Deliverable Forward market used for shorting the rupee is notably associated with which of the following locations?
