92.x: The CCyB ranges from 0 to 2.5 per cent during credit booms. India has had the framework since 2015, but it has not been activated.
92.tq: Distinguish the purpose and activation status of CCyB from other macroprudential tools.
92.sec: Macroprudential tools - purpose

92.s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Tool)
a. Capital conservation buffer
i. Caps total exposure against Tier 1 capital
b. Leverage ratio
ii. Limits loan to a share of collateral value
c. LTV cap
iii. 2.5 per cent over the minimum under Basel III
d. Risk weights
iv. Raised to cool risky lending such as unsecured consumer credit
Which of the following is the correct answer?
92.x: The capital conservation buffer is 2.5 per cent over the minimum; the leverage ratio caps exposure against Tier 1 capital; LTV caps relate loans to collateral; risk weights can cool risky lending.
92.tq: Start from the sure LTV-collateral pair and complete the regulatory-tool matches.
92.sec: Macroprudential tools - purpose

92.s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Capital conservation buffer — 0 to 2.5 per cent activated during every credit boom
Risk weights — raised for unsecured consumer credit in November 2023
LTV caps — housing and gold loans
Leverage ratio — 3 per cent under Basel III
92.x: The 0–2.5 per cent range relates to the countercyclical capital buffer, not the capital conservation buffer. The capital conservation buffer is 2.5 per cent over the minimum.
92.tq: Separate two similarly named capital buffers by their figures and purpose.
92.sec: Macroprudential tools - purpose

92.s: Under Basel III, which combination is correctly stated?
o: Tier 1 capital 2.5 per cent, total CRAR 3 per cent, with only the disclosure pillar
Tier 1 capital 3 per cent, total CRAR 17.3 per cent, with no supervision pillar
Tier 1 capital 9.5 per cent, total CRAR 4.5 per cent, without liquidity ratios
Tier 1 capital 4.5 per cent, total CRAR 9.5 per cent, with LCR and NSFR liquidity ratios
92.x: Basel III specifies Tier 1 capital of 4.5 per cent and total CRAR of 9.5 per cent, along with LCR and NSFR liquidity ratios.
92.tq: Use the paired capital figures and liquidity-ratio clues to identify the complete Basel III combination.
92.sec: Macroprudential tools - purpose

92.s: The three pillars of Basel III mentioned in the framework are:
o: Supervision, deposit insurance and fiscal policy
92.x: The three pillars are capital, supervision and disclosure.
92.tq: Recall the exact three-part regulatory framework.
92.sec: Macroprudential tools - purpose

92.s: Which of the following statements regarding PMC Bank is correct?
o: It failed because of the collapse of the Thai baht and short-term foreign debt.
It was placed under SBI-led reconstruction because of US sub-prime mortgages.
It was an NBFC governed exclusively by SEBI.
Its failure was associated with hidden exposure to one realty group and weakened oversight under dual control.
92.x: PMC Bank had hidden exposure to one realty group, while dual control by the RBI and state Registrars weakened oversight.
92.tq: Combine the institution-specific cause with the regulatory weakness.
92.sec: Cooperative bank failures - PMC Bank, BR Amendment 2020

92.s: The Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act, 2020 brought which institutions under RBI supervision?
o: Only payment banks and small finance banks
All insurance companies and mutual funds
Only foreign banks operating in India
92.x: The 2020 amendment brought urban and multi-state cooperative banks under RBI supervision.
92.tq: Identify the precise institutional coverage of the amendment.
92.sec: Cooperative bank failures - PMC Bank, BR Amendment 2020

92.s: The deposit insurance limit applicable under the stated cooperative-bank framework is:
92.x: Deposit insurance is available up to ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank through DICGC.
92.tq: Recall the exact insurance ceiling and its unit of application.
92.sec: Cooperative bank failures - PMC Bank, BR Amendment 2020

92.s: Prompt Corrective Action primarily monitors weak banks on which of the following parameters?
o: Gold holdings, tax revenue and fiscal deficit
Capital, asset quality including NPA, and leverage
Share prices, dividends and foreign exchange reserves only
Exports, imports and current account balance
92.x: PCA monitors capital, asset quality including NPAs, and leverage, and may impose restrictions on lending, branches and dividends.
92.tq: Identify the supervisory indicators rather than the possible restrictions.
92.sec: Stress tests and early warning - RBI supervisory framework

92.s: Which one of the following is a possible restriction under Prompt Corrective Action?
o: Automatic conversion into a cooperative bank
Compulsory merger with an NBFC in every case
Restrictions on lending, opening branches and declaring dividends
92.x: PCA can impose restrictions on lending, branch expansion and dividend payments, depending on the bank's weakness.
92.tq: Match the supervisory trigger with the practical corrective measures.
92.sec: Stress tests and early warning - RBI supervisory framework

92.s:
Consider the following statements regarding RBI's supervisory framework:
1. Macro stress tests are included in each Financial Stability Report.
2. CRILC is a database for large credits.
3. RBI has issued data-governance guidance for banks.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
92.x: All three statements correctly describe elements of RBI's supervisory and financial-stability framework.
92.tq: Use the comprehensive option when all three supervisory functions are correctly stated.
92.sec: Stress tests and early warning - RBI supervisory framework

92.s: Which one of the following correctly represents the banking-sector health indicators given for the specified periods?
o: GNPA 0.5 per cent and NNPA 17.3 per cent in March 2025; CRAR 2.2 per cent in September 2025
GNPA 2.2 per cent and NNPA 17.3 per cent in September 2025; CRAR 0.5 per cent in March 2025
GNPA 17.3 per cent and NNPA 2.2 per cent in September 2025; CRAR 0.5 per cent in March 2025
GNPA 2.2 per cent and NNPA 0.5 per cent in September 2025; CRAR 17.3 per cent in March 2025
92.x: GNPA was 2.2 per cent and NNPA 0.5 per cent in September 2025, while CRAR was 17.3 per cent in March 2025; the GNPA and NNPA levels were multi-decadal lows.
92.tq: Keep the indicators, percentages and reference dates aligned rather than swapping them.
92.sec: Stress tests and early warning - RBI supervisory framework

92.s: Which of the following risks was flagged in the Financial Stability Report released in June 2026?
o: Risk from falling foreign exchange reserves
92.x: The June 2026 Financial Stability Report flagged risks associated with unsecured lending through fintech platforms.
92.tq: Directly identify the specific risk associated with the named report and date.
92.sec: Universal angles

92.s: The Financial Stability Report of June 2026 highlighted fintech-related risk primarily in the area of:
92.x: The report highlighted risks arising from fintech unsecured lending, rather than from secured housing finance or the other listed areas.
92.tq: Discriminate between closely related forms of lending.
92.sec: Universal angles

92.s: The credit-deposit ratio of Andhra Pradesh was reported as 157.40 per cent. What does this most directly indicate?
o: The State had no dependence on bank deposits for lending.
Banks accepted 157.40 per cent more deposits than they lent.
Bank lending was very high relative to deposits.
Deposits were 157.40 per cent of bank credit.
92.x: A credit-deposit ratio of 157.40 per cent indicates that lending was very high relative to deposits in Andhra Pradesh. It does not mean that deposits exceeded credit.
92.tq: Interpret the direction and meaning of a ratio rather than reversing its numerator and denominator.
92.sec: Universal angles

92.s: Which one of the following correctly represents the regulatory arrangement in the Indian financial system?
o: IRDAI regulates banks and NBFCs, while RBI regulates insurers and FSDC regulates only stock exchanges.
RBI regulates banks and NBFCs, IRDAI regulates insurers, and FSDC coordinates among financial regulators.
RBI regulates insurers, IRDAI regulates banks and NBFCs, and FSDC regulates all financial institutions.
FSDC independently regulates banks, NBFCs and insurers, while RBI performs only a coordinating role.
92.x: The RBI regulates banks and NBFCs, IRDAI regulates insurers, and the Financial Stability and Development Council coordinates among the financial regulators. FSDC is a coordinating body rather than the direct regulator of all these entities.
92.tq: Compare the regulator associated with each segment and distinguish regulation from coordination.
92.sec: Universal angles

93.s: Which one of the following best describes headline inflation?
o: Inflation covering the entire Consumer Price Index basket, including food and fuel
Inflation caused exclusively by excess demand
Inflation excluding food and fuel prices
Inflation measured only through wholesale prices
93.x: Headline inflation covers the whole CPI basket, including volatile food and fuel prices. It is therefore the raw figure generally felt by consumers.
93.tq: Use the exact distinction between headline and core inflation.

93.s:
Consider the following statements regarding core inflation:
1. It generally excludes food and fuel prices.
2. It reflects the underlying demand-side trend in prices.
3. It includes all volatile items so that temporary supply shocks are fully represented.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
93.x: Core inflation excludes food and fuel and is used to indicate the underlying trend, particularly the demand-side trend. Statement 3 is false because volatile items are generally excluded.
93.tq: Find the statement that reverses the meaning of a paired term.

93.s: Food inflation in India is measured through the Consumer Food Price Index (CFPI). How many sub-groups are included in the CFPI classification referred to here?
93.x: The CFPI classification contains 10 sub-groups: cereals, meat and fish, egg, milk, oils, fruits, vegetables, pulses, sugar and spices.
93.tq: Recall the specific quantitative detail rather than the general definition.

93.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (CFPI sub-group)
a. Cereals
a. Meat and fish
c. Pulses
d. Spices

List-II
 i. Food grains
 ii. Animal-source food
 iii. Legumes
 iv. Condiments

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
93.x: Cereals correspond to food grains, meat and fish to animal-source food, pulses to legumes, and spices to condiments.
93.tq: Start from the sure pair and eliminate codes containing a swapped pair.

93.s: Demand-pull inflation is most directly associated with which of the following situations?
o: A fall in wages and raw-material prices
A general fall in the price level
A fall in purchasing power caused by deflation
93.x: Demand-pull inflation occurs when aggregate demand exceeds aggregate supply. Expansionary fiscal policy, loose money and higher purchasing power can contribute to it.
93.tq: Identify whether the pressure originates on the demand side or the supply side.

93.s: Which one of the following is NOT generally a demand-side factor causing inflation?
o: A rise in fuel and raw-material costs
93.x: Higher fuel and raw-material costs are input-cost pressures and therefore cause cost-push inflation. Public expenditure, loose monetary policy and higher incomes can raise aggregate demand.
93.tq: Find the option belonging to the opposite causal category.

93.s:
Assertion (A): Cost-push inflation can occur even when aggregate demand is not unusually strong.
Reason (R): Rising wages, fuel prices or raw-material costs can reduce supply and raise prices.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
93.x: Both statements are true. Cost-push inflation originates from higher input costs, which can reduce supply and increase the prices of goods and services.
93.tq: Test whether the stated supply-side reason directly explains the assertion.

93.s: A rise in wages, fuel prices and other input costs, accompanied by a fall in supply, is characteristic of:
93.x: Cost-push inflation results from increasing input costs such as wages, raw materials and fuel, which put upward pressure on prices through the supply side.
93.tq: Match the named inflation type with its defining cause.

93.s:
Which of the following combinations is associated with supply shocks affecting inflation in India?
1. Erratic monsoon and El Niño
2. Crude oil price movements
3. Rupee depreciation
4. Higher storage and distribution efficiency
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
93.x: Erratic monsoons, El Niño, crude oil price increases and rupee depreciation can create supply-side inflationary pressures. Higher storage and distribution efficiency generally mitigate such pressures.
93.tq: Reject the statement that changes a cause into a remedy.

93.s: The inflationary impact of the West Asia conflict in 2026 was mainly associated with increases in:
93.x: The West Asia conflict in 2026 pushed up fuel and input costs, thereby creating cost-push inflationary pressure.
93.tq: Link the event with its immediate economic transmission channel.

93.s: Stagflation refers to the simultaneous occurrence of:
o: High inflation, stagnant growth and unemployment
High inflation and rapid economic growth
Low inflation and rising industrial production
93.x: Stagflation combines high inflation with stagnant economic growth and unemployment.
93.tq: Use the compound meaning of the term to identify the correct combination.

93.s:
Consider the following as possible drivers of stagflation in India:
1. Higher government spending generating inflationary pressure
2. A fall in industrial output
3. Slow economic growth
4. A sustained rise in productive capacity
Which of the statements given above are correct?
93.x: Stagflation may result when higher government spending adds to inflation while industrial output falls and growth slows. A sustained rise in productive capacity is not a stated driver of stagflation.
93.tq: Separate the combination of inflationary pressure from stagnationary conditions.

93.s: Inflation in only a few commodities, such as food, while overall inflation remains low is known as:
93.x: Skewflation describes a situation in which prices rise sharply in a few items while prices of other items remain stable and overall inflation is low.
93.tq: Discriminate between similar inflation labels by examining their scope.

93.s: If the inflation rate falls from 3 per cent to 2 per cent while the general price level continues to rise, the situation is called:
93.x: Disinflation is a decline in the rate of inflation while inflation remains positive. It is not the same as a fall in the general price level.
93.tq: Distinguish a fall in the inflation rate from a fall in prices themselves.

93.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes deflation from disinflation?
o: Deflation is a fall in the general price level, whereas disinflation is a fall in the inflation rate that remains positive
Deflation is a fall in the inflation rate with prices still rising, whereas disinflation is negative inflation
Deflation affects only food prices, whereas disinflation affects only fuel prices
Deflation follows reflation, whereas disinflation necessarily causes reflation
93.x: Deflation means a fall in the general price level and represents negative inflation. Disinflation means that the inflation rate falls but remains positive.
93.tq: Compare the direction of the price level with the direction of the inflation rate.

93.s: Inflation returning after a period of deflation, generally indicating economic recovery, is termed:
93.x: Reflation refers to the return of inflation after deflation and is regarded as a sign of recovery.
93.tq: Use the prefix and the stated economic sequence to identify the term.

93.s: Structural shortages arising from poor farm productivity, inadequate storage and weak distribution are associated with:
93.x: Bottleneck inflation is caused by structural supply constraints, including poor farm productivity and inadequate storage and distribution.
93.tq: Match the inflation type with its structural supply constraint.

93.s: Export-led inflation may occur when:
o: Strong export demand drains domestic supply and pushes domestic prices upward
The inflation rate declines but remains positive
Imports increase domestic supply and lower prices
The general price level falls because demand is postponed
93.x: Strong export demand can divert goods away from the domestic market, reduce domestic availability and raise domestic prices.
93.tq: Trace the effect of exports on domestic availability and prices.

93.s:
Arrange the following types of inflation in ascending order according to the approximate annual rate indicated:
A. Walking or trotting inflation
B. Creeping inflation
C. Hyperinflation
D. Galloping inflation
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
93.x: Creeping inflation is below 3 per cent, walking or trotting inflation is around 3–10 per cent, and galloping inflation precedes hyperinflation in severity.
93.tq: First place the category with the stated numerical range, then order the extreme categories by intensity.

93.s: Walking or trotting inflation is generally understood as inflation of approximately:
93.x: Walking or trotting inflation is around 3–10 per cent per year. Inflation below 3 per cent is described as creeping inflation.
93.tq: Use the stated range to eliminate adjacent inflation categories.

93.s:
Which of the following can contribute to inflationary pressure in India?
1. Hoarding
2. Increases in minimum support prices
3. Inflation expectations
4. A permanent fall in all input costs
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
93.x: Hoarding, MSP increases and inflation expectations can add to inflationary pressure. A permanent fall in all input costs would generally reduce cost-push pressure.
93.tq: Identify the three stated inflationary pressures and reject the reversed cost effect.

93.s: Which measure was associated with easing cereal prices in the context of Bharat Atta?
o: Bharat Atta helped ease cereal prices
Bharat Atta excluded cereals from the CPI basket
Bharat Atta caused hyperinflation in cereals
Bharat Atta increased cereal prices through export demand
93.x: The stated assessment was that Bharat Atta helped ease cereal prices, thereby moderating cereal-price pressure.
93.tq: Identify the policy measure's direction of impact rather than its general sector.

93.s: Inflation has which of the following effects on the purchasing power of money?
o: It reduces purchasing power because the same amount of money buys fewer goods and services
It increases purchasing power because nominal incomes always rise faster than prices
It leaves purchasing power unchanged in all circumstances
93.x: When prices rise, a given amount of money purchases fewer goods and services. Thus inflation lowers the purchasing power of money.
93.tq: Apply the price–purchasing-power inverse relationship.

93.s: A rising GNP or GDP deflator, other things remaining equal, generally implies:
o: No change in the general price level
An increase in the purchasing power of money
A decrease in the purchasing power of money
A fall in nominal prices only
93.x: A rising GNP or GDP deflator indicates a higher general price level. Consequently, the purchasing power of money decreases.
93.tq: Read a deflator as a broad price-level indicator and infer its purchasing-power effect.

93.s: Which one of the following groups is most likely to gain from inflation?
o: Debtors and holders of real assets
93.x: Debtors repay loans in money with lower real value, while holders of real assets may benefit from rising prices. Creditors and fixed-income groups generally lose.
93.tq: Apply the distinction between nominal repayment and real value.

93.s:
Consider the following statements about the distributional effects of inflation:
1. Debtors may gain because the real value of their repayment falls.
2. Creditors may lose because the money received has lower purchasing power.
3. Fixed-income groups such as pensioners are generally protected automatically from inflation.
4. Holders of real assets may gain from rising prices.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
93.x: Debtors and real-asset holders may gain, while creditors and fixed-income groups may lose. Statement 3 is false because fixed-income groups are generally vulnerable unless their incomes are adjusted.
93.tq: Find the single statement that reverses the usual distributional effect.

93.s: Food inflation is considered regressive primarily because:
o: Food inflation benefits fixed-income households most
Food forms a relatively large share of the expenditure of poorer households
Food is excluded from the CPI basket
Food prices are unaffected by supply shocks
93.x: Food inflation is regressive because poorer households spend a larger share of their income on food. Food and beverages account for approximately 37 per cent of the CPI basket.
93.tq: Connect the incidence of inflation with the expenditure pattern of vulnerable groups.

93.s: Approximately what share of the CPI basket is represented by food and beverages in the context of food inflation's regressive effect?
93.x: Food and beverages account for approximately 37 per cent of the CPI basket in the stated classification.
93.tq: Recall the specific percentage and distinguish it from nearby figures.

93.s: Which of the following is NOT a commonly identified cost of inflation?
o: Shoeleather costs arising from managing cash balances
Greater certainty that encourages all investment
93.x: Inflation creates menu costs, shoeleather costs and uncertainty that can discourage investment. It does not necessarily create greater certainty or encourage all investment.
93.tq: Reject the absolute and reversed consequence among otherwise valid costs.

93.s: Deflation can initiate a deflationary spiral because it may lead to which sequence?
o: Postponed purchases, lower profits, higher unemployment and a heavier real debt burden
Immediate purchases, higher profits, lower unemployment and lighter real debt
Higher wages, greater demand, rising output and lower real debt
Higher inflation expectations, increased exports and full employment
93.x: During deflation, consumers may postpone purchases, causing profits and production to fall; unemployment can rise and the real burden of debt increases.
93.tq: Follow the causal chain from falling prices to demand, profits, employment and debt.

93.s:
Assertion (A): Deflation increases the purchasing power of money.
Reason (R): A fall in the general price level enables a given amount of money to buy more goods and services.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
93.x: Both statements are true, and the reason directly explains why deflation raises purchasing power. However, deflation may also produce a damaging spiral of reduced demand and employment.
93.tq: Check whether the reason directly establishes the purchasing-power effect.

93.s: The CPI (Rural/Urban/Combined) in India is published by which organisation?
o: National Statistical Office, Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation
Office of the Economic Adviser, DPIIT
93.x: The CPI for Rural, Urban and Combined sectors is published by the National Statistical Office under the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation.
93.tq: Identify the institution associated with the index rather than confusing it with the WPI publisher.
93.sec: Price indices - publisher, base year, weights

93.s: The current base year of the new CPI (Rural/Urban/Combined) series is
93.x: The new CPI series uses 2024 as its base year and was introduced from the earlier 2012-based series.
93.tq: Use the latest base year and distinguish it from the earlier CPI series.
93.sec: Price indices - publisher, base year, weights

93.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the new CPI series:
1. Its weights are derived from the Household Consumption Expenditure Survey 2023-24.
2. It has 12 divisions based on COICOP 2018.
3. The earlier CPI structure had six groups.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
93.x: All three statements are correct: the new CPI uses HCES 2023-24 weights, follows 12 COICOP 2018 divisions and replaces the earlier six-group structure.
93.tq: Check whether all the structural changes belong to the same revised index series.
93.sec: Price indices - publisher, base year, weights

93.s: How many items are included in the new CPI basket, and how are they divided between goods and services?
93.x: The new CPI basket contains 358 items, comprising 308 goods and 50 services.
93.tq: Match the total with its component figures before selecting the numerical option.
93.sec: Price indices - publisher, base year, weights

93.s: Which of the following correctly states the weights of food and beverages and housing in the new CPI basket?
93.x: Food and beverages have a weight of 36.75% and housing has a weight of 17.67% in the new CPI basket.
93.tq: Discriminate between closely related percentage figures and their categories.
93.sec: Price indices - publisher, base year, weights

93.s: Which of the following features was added to the new CPI series?
o: Services were removed from the basket
Rural house rent and 12 online platforms
Urban house rent and 12 manufacturing groups
93.x: Rural house rent and 12 online platforms were added to the new CPI series.
93.tq: Select the precise combination of additions instead of an extreme or reversed statement.
93.sec: Price indices - publisher, base year, weights

93.s: The current base year of the Wholesale Price Index series is
93.x: The current WPI series has 2022-23 as its base year and replaced the earlier 2011-12 base.
93.tq: Separate the current base year from an earlier officially used base year.
93.sec: Price indices - publisher, base year, weights

93.s:
With reference to the new WPI series, consider the following statements:
1. It contains 957 items.
2. The earlier series contained 697 items.
3. Its weights are based on Gross Value of Output.
4. It covers services along with goods.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
93.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 4 is false because WPI covers goods and does not cover services.
93.tq: Find the single false statement by testing the coverage of the index separately from its numerical details.
93.sec: Price indices - publisher, base year, weights

93.s: The proposed relationship between the new WPI and the Producer Price Index is that
o: PPI will run alongside WPI for five years, after which WPI will be phased out
WPI will cover services only after PPI is introduced
Both indices will be permanently merged after one year
93.x: The new WPI is intended to run with a new Producer Price Index for five years, after which WPI is to be phased out.
93.tq: Follow the stated sequence of transition instead of reversing the roles of the two indices.
93.sec: Price indices - publisher, base year, weights

93.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
o: GDP deflator — Office of the Economic Adviser — 2022-23 base
93.x: CPI-IW is published by the Labour Bureau and uses 2016 as its base year. The other pairs incorrectly combine publishers or base years.
93.tq: Start from the sure publisher-base pair and eliminate crossed combinations.
93.sec: Price indices - publisher, base year, weights

93.s: The CPI-IW series with 2016 as its base year has been in use since
93.x: The CPI-IW has used the 2016 base since September 2020; the preceding base was 2001.
93.tq: Distinguish the effective date of a series from the date of a later CPI revision.
93.sec: Price indices - publisher, base year, weights

93.s: Which of the following statements regarding CPI-AL and CPI-RL is correct?
o: CPI-AL has a 2011-12 base, whereas CPI-RL has a 2022-23 base.
CPI-AL has a 2019 base from June 2025, whereas CPI-RL is listed with the 1986-87 base.
CPI-AL is published by NSO and CPI-RL by DPIIT.
Both CPI-AL and CPI-RL have a 2024 base from February 2026.
93.x: CPI-AL moved to a 2019 base from June 2025, while CPI-RL is listed with the 1986-87 base. Both are published by the Labour Bureau.
93.tq: Separate the two similar labour-sector indices by their stated base years.
93.sec: Price indices - publisher, base year, weights

93.s: The linking factor for CPI-AL is stated as
o: 10.72 for both Andhra Pradesh and India
10.72 for India and 9.69 for Andhra Pradesh
9.69 for Andhra Pradesh and 10.72 for India
10.72 for Andhra Pradesh and 9.69 for India
93.x: The linking factor for CPI-AL is 10.72 for Andhra Pradesh and 9.69 for India.
93.tq: Read the geographical labels carefully before matching each figure.
93.sec: Price indices - publisher, base year, weights

93.s: CPI-IW is primarily used for determining the dearness allowance of
93.x: CPI-IW is used for determining dearness allowance for industrial workers.
93.tq: Link the specialised index to the category of workers it represents.
93.sec: Price indices - publisher, base year, weights

93.s: Which of the following correctly compares CPI and WPI?
o: CPI measures producer prices of goods only, whereas WPI measures retail prices of goods and services.
CPI measures retail prices of goods and services, whereas WPI measures first-point bulk sale prices of goods only.
Both CPI and WPI measure only retail prices of goods.
Both CPI and WPI include services with identical weights.
93.x: CPI measures consumer retail prices and includes goods and services. WPI measures first-point bulk sale or producer-level prices and covers goods only.
93.tq: Split the comparison into price level and coverage before choosing the complete pair.
93.sec: Price indices - publisher, base year, weights

93.s: Which index is regarded as the broadest measure because it covers all goods and services produced in the economy?
93.x: The GDP deflator is the broadest measure because it covers all goods and services produced in the economy, including services.
93.tq: Use the coverage clue to distinguish the economy-wide deflator from price-basket indices.
93.sec: Price indices - publisher, base year, weights

93.s: The GDP deflator is calculated as
o: Real GDP multiplied by nominal GDP divided by 100
Nominal GDP divided by real GDP multiplied by 100
Nominal GDP minus real GDP divided by 100
Real GDP divided by nominal GDP multiplied by 100
93.x: GDP deflator equals nominal GDP divided by real GDP, multiplied by 100. A rise in the deflator reduces the purchasing power of money.
93.tq: Recall the numerator-denominator order in the formula rather than reversing it.
93.sec: Price indices - publisher, base year, weights

93.s: A rise in the GDP deflator, other things remaining the same, indicates a reduction in the
93.x: An increase in the GDP deflator reflects a rise in the general price level and therefore reduces the purchasing power of money.
93.tq: Translate the movement of a price index into its effect on money value.
93.sec: Price indices - publisher, base year, weights

93.s:
Arrange the following developments in the correct chronological order:
A. RBI adopted CPI (Combined) as its key inflation measure
B. Monetary Policy Framework Agreement
C. Amendment of the RBI Act providing the statutory framework
D. First invocation of the report requirement after breach of the inflation band
93.x: The sequence is CPI adoption in April 2014, the February 2015 Monetary Policy Framework Agreement, the 2016 RBI Act amendment and the first invocation in 2022.
93.tq: Fix the earliest event and then place the agreement, legislation and later invocation.
93.sec: Index used for measuring inflation - headline measure and the switch

93.s: Before the adoption of CPI (Combined) by the RBI in April 2014, India used which index as the headline inflation measure?
93.x: WPI was earlier used as India's headline inflation measure. The RBI adopted CPI (Combined) as its key measure in April 2014 following the Urjit Patel Committee framework.
93.tq: Test the before-and-after distinction in a policy transition.
93.sec: Index used for measuring inflation - headline measure and the switch

93.s: Which of the following provisions is correctly matched with the RBI Act, 1934 as amended in 2016?
o: Section 45ZA — constitution of the six-member MPC
Section 45ZB — inflation target fixed by the Centre with RBI every five years
Section 45ZN — report to be made when the inflation band is breached for three consecutive quarters
93.x: Section 45ZN requires a report when the inflation band is breached for three consecutive quarters. Section 45ZA concerns the target-setting process, while Section 45ZB concerns the MPC.
93.tq: Match each statutory section with its specific function instead of relying on the common subject matter.
93.sec: Index used for measuring inflation - headline measure and the switch

93.s:
Consider the following statements about India's flexible inflation-targeting framework:
1. The inflation target is fixed by the Centre in consultation with the RBI every five years.
2. The Monetary Policy Committee consists of six members.
3. A breach of the tolerance band for three consecutive quarters requires the RBI to report its reasons to the Government.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
93.x: All three statements correctly describe the flexible inflation-targeting framework under the amended RBI Act.
93.tq: Check the target-setting, MPC composition and breach-reporting provisions together.
93.sec: Index used for measuring inflation - headline measure and the switch

93.s: For the period from 1 April 2026 to 31 March 2031, the CPI-based inflation target is
93.x: The retained target is 4% with a tolerance band of plus or minus 2% for 1 April 2026 to 31 March 2031.
93.tq: Distinguish the central target from the width of the tolerance band.
93.sec: Index used for measuring inflation - headline measure and the switch

93.s: Which of the following is correctly matched with its principal use?
o: CPI — contract escalation only; WPI — dearness allowance only
CPI — dearness allowance; WPI — contract escalation and industrial analysis
CPI-IW — Producer Price Index; WPI — rural wage revision only
GDP deflator — industrial workers' dearness allowance; CPI — producer prices
93.x: CPI is also used for dearness allowance, while WPI is used for contract escalation and industrial analysis.
93.tq: Associate each index with its practical institutional use without reversing the pair.
93.sec: Index used for measuring inflation - headline measure and the switch

93.s: Which statement best reflects the policy debate concerning the inflation target?
o: The debate concerns only the choice between WPI and GDP deflator.
Core inflation is stickier and responds more to policy, leading to debate over whether the target should be headline or core inflation.
Headline inflation excludes food and energy, while core inflation includes them.
Core inflation is more volatile than headline inflation and responds less to policy.
93.x: The debate is whether policy should target headline or core inflation; core inflation is considered stickier and more responsive to policy.
93.tq: Choose the option that states both the nature of core inflation and the actual policy issue.
93.sec: Index used for measuring inflation - headline measure and the switch

93.s: In May 2026, the relative ordering of food, headline and core inflation was
93.x: In May 2026, food inflation was 4.85%, headline inflation was 3.93% and core inflation was 3.73%, giving the order Food > Headline > Core.
93.tq: Arrange the three measures by comparing their actual percentages.
93.sec: Relative ordering of food, headline and core inflation

93.s: Which of the following correctly represents the inflation figures for May 2026 under the new CPI series?
93.x: The May 2026 figures were 3.93% headline inflation, 4.85% food inflation and 3.73% core inflation.
93.tq: Keep the indicator labels attached to the figures when comparing close percentages.
93.sec: Relative ordering of food, headline and core inflation

93.s: The first breach of the 4% CPI inflation target in the new series occurred in
93.x: Headline CPI inflation reached 4.38% in June 2026, marking the first breach of the 4% target.
93.tq: Distinguish the first threshold breach from later higher readings.
93.sec: Relative ordering of food, headline and core inflation

93.s: Which of the following statements regarding July 2026 inflation is correct?
o: Headline CPI inflation was 4.45%, rural food inflation was 5.79%, and core inflation was below 3% excluding precious metals.
Headline CPI inflation was 3.93%, rural food inflation was 4.85%, and core inflation exceeded 5%.
Headline CPI inflation was 4.38%, rural food inflation was 5.05%, and core inflation was exactly 4%.
Headline CPI inflation was 4.80%, rural food inflation was 5.70%, and core inflation was above 4.45%.
93.x: In July 2026, headline CPI inflation was 4.45%, rural food inflation was 5.79%, and core inflation was below 3% when precious metals were excluded.
93.tq: Match the month with all three indicators and reject figures belonging to adjacent months.
93.sec: Relative ordering of food, headline and core inflation

93.s: Headline CPI inflation reached a 20-month high of 4.8% in
93.x: Headline CPI inflation reached 4.8% in August 2026, described as a 20-month high.
93.tq: Use the time descriptor to identify the correct monthly observation.
93.sec: Relative ordering of food, headline and core inflation

93.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the inflation position during 2025?
o: CPI inflation was 1.7%, while food inflation was minus 0.2%.
CPI inflation was 3.88%, while food inflation was 2.2%.
CPI inflation was 2.2%, a 12-year low, while food inflation was minus 0.2%.
CPI inflation was 6.7%, while food inflation was 2.2%.
93.x: In 2025, CPI inflation was 2.2%, a 12-year low, and food inflation was −0.2%.
93.tq: Separate the annual figures from the later financial-year and WPI figures.
93.sec: Relative ordering of food, headline and core inflation

93.s: The order of inflation measures recorded for 2025 was
93.x: For 2025, the stated order was Core > Headline > Food, with headline CPI at 2.2% and food inflation at −0.2%.
93.tq: Use the negative food-inflation figure to place food at the end of the order.
93.sec: Relative ordering of food, headline and core inflation

93.s: Food inflation of −0.2% in 2025 was described as
93.x: The −0.2% food inflation recorded in 2025 was described as the first food deflation since 2014.
93.tq: Treat the reference year as a separate chronological fact rather than confusing it with the CPI base year.
93.sec: Relative ordering of food, headline and core inflation

93.s: The lowest CPI inflation recorded in October 2025 was
o: 1.7%, the lowest in the financial year
93.x: CPI inflation was 0.3% in October 2025, the lowest recorded in the 2012 series.
93.tq: Distinguish the monthly low from the annual low and from the series base year.
93.sec: Relative ordering of food, headline and core inflation

93.s: According to the Economic Survey 2025-26 figures, CPI inflation fell from 6.7% in FY23 to what level during April–December FY26?
93.x: The CPI inflation rate fell from 6.7% in FY23 to 1.7% during April–December FY26.
93.tq: Identify the period attached to the figure instead of selecting the nearby annual or WPI rate.
93.sec: Relative ordering of food, headline and core inflation

93.s: The WPI inflation rate reached a 38-month high of 3.88% in
93.x: WPI inflation rose to a 38-month high of 3.88% in March 2026.
93.tq: Separate the WPI observation from the monthly CPI observations of June to August.
93.sec: Relative ordering of food, headline and core inflation

93.s: Which explanation was given for WPI inflation being far above CPI inflation in June and July 2026?
o: The inclusion of services in the WPI basket
Higher fuel costs associated with the West Asia conflict
A change in the CPI base year alone
A sharp fall in manufactured-goods prices due to domestic oversupply
93.x: WPI inflation was 9.87% in June and 9.78% in July 2026, far above CPI inflation mainly because of fuel costs associated with the West Asia conflict.
93.tq: Link the observed divergence between indices to the stated sector-specific cause.
93.sec: Relative ordering of food, headline and core inflation

93.s: The WPI inflation rates for June and July 2026 were, respectively
93.x: WPI inflation was 9.87% in June 2026 and 9.78% in July 2026.
93.tq: Preserve the month-wise order when two close numerical values are given.
93.sec: Relative ordering of food, headline and core inflation

93.s: Who first established an inverse relationship between unemployment and wage inflation in 1958?
93.x: A.W. Phillips established the inverse relationship between unemployment and wage inflation in 1958.
93.tq: Direct recall of the economist associated with a concept and year.

93.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Phillips curve:
1. In the short run, lower unemployment is generally associated with higher inflation.
2. In the long run, the Phillips curve is vertical according to Friedman.
3. The long-run Phillips curve implies a lasting trade-off between inflation and unemployment.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
93.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. The long-run vertical curve indicates that there is no lasting trade-off between inflation and unemployment, making statement 3 false.
93.tq: Separate the short-run relationship from the long-run qualification.

93.s: The Phillips curve observed in India during 2012–2026 has been described as relatively flat primarily because:
o: The Reserve Bank of India fixes all wages
The formal workforce has complete wage flexibility
Around 92% of workers are informal and have weak wage-bargaining power
Food prices are excluded from the CPI
93.x: India’s relatively flat Phillips curve is linked to the large informal workforce, estimated at about 92%, whose weak wage-bargaining power prevents wages from responding strongly to output changes.
93.tq: Link the observed macroeconomic outcome with its structural cause.

93.s: Which of the following best describes the stagflation risk associated with raising interest rates when inflation is supply-driven?
o: Interest-rate hikes necessarily reduce prices without affecting output
Interest-rate hikes increase employment and eliminate supply constraints
Interest-rate hikes affect only exports and not domestic demand
Interest-rate hikes may reduce output and employment without substantially lowering inflation
93.x: A repo-rate increase is primarily a demand-side measure. When inflation arises from supply shocks, it may reduce output and jobs without significantly lowering prices.
93.tq: Apply the demand-side versus supply-side distinction to a policy scenario.

93.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
o: Monetary measure — sale of securities through open market operations
Fiscal measure — release of onion buffer stocks by NCCF
Supply-side measure — increase in cash reserve ratio
Monetary measure — reduction of indirect taxes on essential goods
93.x: Sale of securities through open market operations is a monetary measure. Buffer-stock release is supply-side, while taxes and government spending are fiscal instruments.
93.tq: Classify each instrument by identifying the authority and channel through which it works.

93.s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Fiscal policy — tightening liquidity through open market sales
Fiscal policy — reducing the fiscal deficit
Monetary policy — raising the repo rate
93.x: Tightening liquidity through open market sales is a monetary measure undertaken by the RBI, not a fiscal measure.
93.tq: Find the instrument placed under the wrong policy category.

93.s: The principal purpose of selling securities through open market operations during inflationary conditions is to:
o: Raise the minimum export price of onions
Increase liquidity in the banking system
Tighten liquidity in the banking system
93.x: When the RBI sells securities through OMOs, money is withdrawn from the banking system, thereby tightening liquidity and moderating demand.
93.tq: Identify the immediate monetary transmission channel of an instrument.

93.s:
With reference to supply-side measures for controlling food inflation, consider the following statements:
1. The Food Corporation of India sells wheat and rice at fixed prices under OMSS.
2. The Price Stabilisation Fund maintains buffers of pulses and onions.
3. Bharat Atta, Bharat Rice and Bharat Dal are examples of subsidised sales.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
93.x: All three statements are correct. OMSS sales by FCI, PSF buffers and subsidised Bharat-branded food sales are supply-side responses to food inflation.
93.tq: Use the common policy objective to verify all three supply-side measures.

93.s: Bharat Chana Dal was introduced in July 2023 at which price?
93.x: Bharat Chana Dal was introduced in July 2023 at ₹60 per kilogram.
93.tq: Recall the exact price attached to a subsidised anti-inflation measure.

93.s: Which institution or institutions were involved in releasing onion stocks from the Price Stabilisation Fund buffer?
93.x: NCCF and NAFED released 47,786 metric tonnes of onion from the PSF buffer up to 8 October 2025.
93.tq: Match the operational agencies with the supply-side intervention.

93.s: How much onion was released from the Price Stabilisation Fund buffer by NCCF and NAFED up to 8 October 2025?
93.x: The quantity released from the PSF onion buffer was 47,786 metric tonnes up to 8 October 2025.
93.tq: Test the exact quantity using closely spaced numerical distractors.

93.s: Subsidised sales of Bharat Atta, Bharat Rice and Bharat Dal are made through which combination of agencies?
93.x: These subsidised food products are sold through NAFED, NCCF and Kendriya Bhandar.
93.tq: Recall the distribution agencies rather than the producing authority.

93.s:
Arrange the following developments relating to onion trade policy in chronological order:
A. Onion export ban was lifted with a 40% export duty and a US$550 minimum export price.
B. Minimum export price was removed and export duty was reduced to 20%.
C. Bharat Chana Dal was introduced.

Select the correct sequence.
93.x: Bharat Chana Dal was introduced in July 2023, the onion export ban was lifted on 4 May 2024, and the MEP was removed with duty reduced on 13 September 2024.
93.tq: Place the dated policy changes first and then verify the sequence.

93.s: Which of the following statements regarding onion export policy is correct?
o: The export ban was lifted on 4 May 2024 with a 40% duty and a US$550 MEP; on 13 September 2024 the MEP was removed and duty reduced to 20%.
The export ban was lifted on 4 May 2024 with a 20% duty and no MEP; on 13 September 2024 duty was raised to 40%.
The export ban continued after September 2024, but the MEP was reduced to US$550.
The export ban was lifted in September 2024 with a 40% duty, followed by restoration of the ban in October 2024.
93.x: The ban was lifted on 4 May 2024 subject to a 40% duty and a US$550 MEP. On 13 September 2024, the MEP was removed and the duty was reduced to 20%.
93.tq: Track a policy change by matching both dates and successive conditions.

93.s: In Andhra Pradesh, the State-level Price Monitoring Committee for essential commodities is headed by the:
o: Chairman of the State Public Service Commission
93.x: The Andhra Pradesh State-level Price Monitoring Committee is headed by the Chief Secretary.
93.tq: Identify the senior administrative authority associated with the monitoring mechanism.

93.s: Which of the following statements about price monitoring in Andhra Pradesh is correct?
o: DES monitors eight essential commodities annually, with rice and wheat added in February 2025.
The RBI monitors eight essential commodities daily in Andhra Pradesh.
DES monitors eight essential commodities daily, with groundnut oil and palm oil added in February 2025.
DES monitors only agricultural exports and does not monitor edible oils.
93.x: The Directorate of Economics and Statistics monitors eight essential commodities daily. Groundnut oil and palm oil were added in February 2025.
93.tq: Test the agency, frequency and newly added items together.

93.s: Which one of the following correctly identifies the limitation of using the repo rate to control inflation?
o: It is a supply-side tool and cannot affect demand
It is a demand-side tool and cannot directly resolve shocks such as onion prices or crude-oil prices
It directly fixes the minimum export price of agricultural commodities
It can be used only by the Union Government for reducing food stocks
93.x: The repo rate influences aggregate demand and liquidity, but it cannot directly remove supply shocks such as sudden increases in onion or crude-oil prices.
93.tq: Ask whether the policy instrument addresses the source of the shock.

93.s: The Urjit Patel Committee of 2014 was primarily associated with which of the following?
o: Revision of the WPI series with 2011–12 as base
Revision of the WPI series with 2004–05 as base
Monetary policy framework, CPI as nominal anchor and flexible inflation targeting
93.x: The Urjit Patel Committee recommended a monetary policy framework centred on CPI as the nominal anchor and flexible inflation targeting.
93.tq: Match the committee with its distinctive policy subject.

93.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Committee)
A. Urjit Patel Committee
B. Abhijit Sen Working Group
C. Saumitra Chaudhuri Working Group

List-II (Subject or base)
1. Monetary policy framework and flexible inflation targeting
2. WPI revision with 2004–05 base
3. WPI revision with 2011–12 base

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
93.x: Urjit Patel was associated with the monetary policy framework; Abhijit Sen with the 2004–05 WPI revision; and Saumitra Chaudhuri with the 2011–12 WPI revision.
93.tq: Start with the distinctive committee-policy pair and eliminate conflicting codes.

93.s: Inflation-indexed bonds are securities in which:
o: Only the coupon rate is fixed permanently, irrespective of inflation
Repayment is linked exclusively to the exchange rate
The principal is linked to the stock-market index alone
The principal and/or interest is linked to an inflation index
93.x: In inflation-indexed bonds, the principal and/or interest payments are linked to an inflation index, protecting the investor’s real return.
93.tq: Use the defining contractual feature to distinguish the instrument.

93.s: The Reserve Bank of India issued Inflation-Indexed Bonds in:
93.x: The RBI issued Inflation-Indexed Bonds in 2013.
93.tq: Recall the introduction year using adjacent-year distractors.

93.s: Which of the following is NOT an expected benefit of inflation-indexed bonds?
o: Expanding the investor base for government borrowing
Guaranteeing permanently lower borrowing costs regardless of inflation credibility
Providing investors a hedge against inflation
93.x: Inflation-indexed bonds provide a real-return hedge, can widen the investor base and may shift savings from gold. Cheaper government borrowing depends on credible commitment to low inflation; it is not guaranteed regardless of inflation performance.
93.tq: Reject the absolute claim that ignores the condition attached to cheaper borrowing.

93.s:
Consider the following statements about inflation-indexed bonds:
1. They protect investors against inflation by linking payments to an inflation index.
2. They can signal the government's commitment to maintaining low inflation.
3. They may help shift household savings away from gold.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
93.x: All three statements are correct. Inflation-indexed bonds protect real returns, signal an anti-inflation commitment and offer an alternative to gold savings.
93.tq: Recognise the common investor, government and savings effects of the instrument.

93.s: In August 2026, the repo rate referred to in the monetary-policy discussion was:
93.x: The repo rate was stated as 5.25% in August 2026, with an October hike expected.
93.tq: Test a current policy rate with close percentage-point distractors.

93.s: Which of the following correctly represents the reported August 2026 inflation position in India?
o: CPI about 3.9% and WPI near 4.9%, driven only by manufactured goods
CPI about 9.8% and WPI near 4.8%, driven only by services
CPI about 4.8% and WPI near 1.8%, with no contribution from food
CPI about 4.8% and WPI near 9.8%, driven by fuel and food
93.x: The reported August 2026 figures were CPI at about 4.8% and WPI near 9.8%, with fuel and food identified as major drivers after the West Asia conflict.
93.tq: Keep the index labels and the direction of the comparison aligned.

93.s: Which of the following statements regarding inflation in Andhra Pradesh in May 2026 is correct?
o: AP retail inflation was 4.9%, equal to India’s 4.9%, for the fifth consecutive month.
AP retail inflation was 5.09% in urban areas and 4.61% in rural areas.
AP retail inflation was 3.9%, below India’s 4.9%.
AP retail inflation was 4.9%, above India’s 3.9%, and remained above the national rate for five consecutive months.
93.x: Andhra Pradesh recorded retail inflation of 4.9% against India’s 3.9% in May 2026 and was above the national rate for five consecutive months.
93.tq: Check both the level comparison and the duration claim.

93.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched regarding Andhra Pradesh consumer price indices?
o: CPI-IW centres — Visakhapatnam, Vijayawada and Kurnool
CPI-IW centres — Guntur, Vijayawada and Nellore only
93.x: CPI-AL inflation was 0.81% in Andhra Pradesh against 1.78% for India. The CPI-IW centres identified were Guntur, Visakhapatnam and Nellore, with Vijayawada dropped.
93.tq: Match both figures and locations without swapping their jurisdictions.

93.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the change in the CPI-Combined index?
93.x: The CPI-Combined index increased from 197.9 to 204.9 in Andhra Pradesh and from 192.6 to 198.0 in India.
93.tq: Keep each jurisdiction’s two-point index movement together.

93.s: Following the adoption of flexible inflation targeting, the average CPI inflation reportedly declined from approximately 6.8% during 2012–16 to:
93.x: Average CPI inflation declined from 6.8% during 2012–16 to about 4.9% after flexible inflation targeting.
93.tq: Test the before-and-after policy figures with nearby percentage distractors.

93.s: Which of the following best captures the significance of maintaining low inflation?
o: It necessarily increases the fiscal deficit and discourages foreign investment.
It benefits only exporters and has no effect on poorer households.
It protects the poor and helps anchor the rupee and foreign portfolio investment.
It eliminates all supply shocks and guarantees higher employment.
93.x: Low and stable inflation protects poorer households, supports confidence in the rupee and helps anchor foreign portfolio investment.
93.tq: Select the option that combines the distributional and macro-financial effects.

93.s: Which of the following concerns is associated with inflation targeting based mainly on headline CPI?
o: Headline CPI can be influenced only by fiscal policy
Inflation targeting prevents any change in interest rates
Headline CPI excludes all food and fuel shocks by definition
Most inflation shocks may be supply-driven, while monetary-policy transmission can be slow
93.x: A key criticism is that headline CPI may reflect supply shocks that interest rates cannot quickly resolve, while policy transmission may also be slow.
93.tq: Identify the policy-design criticism arising from the source and transmission of inflation.

93.s:
Consider the following statements regarding inflation in June–July 2026:
1. Headline CPI moved back above 4%.
2. The increase was food-led.
3. Core inflation remained stable.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
93.x: Headline CPI was reported above 4% in June–July 2026, with food as the main driver while core inflation remained stable.
93.tq: Combine the headline movement, principal driver and core-inflation condition.

94.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the principal distinction between direct and indirect taxes in India?
o: In a direct tax, impact and incidence fall on the same person, whereas the burden of an indirect tax can be shifted to the consumer
In a direct tax, the burden is shifted through prices, whereas an indirect tax cannot be shifted
Direct taxes are collected by intermediaries, whereas indirect taxes are collected by the income-tax authorities
Both direct and indirect taxes are collected only from the final consumer
94.x: The impact and incidence of a direct tax fall on the same person and cannot ordinarily be shifted. An indirect tax is collected through an intermediary and passed on to the consumer through the price.
94.tq: Split the options by checking whether the tax burden can be shifted.
94.sec: Direct vs indirect taxes - classification and base  [APPSC]

94.s: With reference to the administration of taxation in India, which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Direct taxes — Central Board of Direct Taxes
Direct taxes — Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs
Indirect taxes — Central Board of Direct Taxes
Both direct and indirect taxes — Central Board of Direct Taxes
94.x: Direct taxes are administered by the Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT), while indirect taxes are administered by the Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC).
94.tq: Use the authority-swap trap by matching each tax category with its administering body.
94.sec: Direct vs indirect taxes - classification and base  [APPSC]

94.s: The base of corporation tax in India is principally the:
o: Value of goods manufactured by companies
Market value of shares issued by companies
94.x: Corporation tax is levied on the net profit of companies. Its base rate is 22%, with an effective rate of approximately 25.17%.
94.tq: Distinguish the tax base from turnover, share value and production value.
94.sec: Direct vs indirect taxes - classification and base  [APPSC]

94.s: Which one of the following statements regarding wealth tax is correct?
o: It was imposed on the annual income of individuals and introduced in 2004
It was levied on net wealth, introduced in 1957 and abolished in 2015
It was levied on securities traded on stock exchanges and abolished in 2017
It was an indirect tax on imported wealth and abolished in 1991
94.x: Wealth tax was a direct tax on net wealth. It was introduced in 1957 and abolished in 2015.
94.tq: Check the tax base first and then verify the introduction and abolition years.
94.sec: Direct vs indirect taxes - classification and base  [APPSC]

94.s: Securities Transaction Tax (STT) is a direct tax levied on the:
o: Value of securities traded on stock exchanges
Capital goods imported through stock exchanges
94.x: STT is classified as a direct tax and is levied on the value of securities traded on stock exchanges. It has been in force from 1 October 2004.
94.tq: Use the exact base and commencement date to separate STT from other financial taxes.
94.sec: Direct vs indirect taxes - classification and base  [APPSC]

94.s: GST was introduced in India with effect from:
94.x: GST, an indirect tax on the supply of goods and services, came into effect on 1 July 2017.
94.tq: Discriminate among the nearby dates associated with tax reforms and financial measures.
94.sec: Direct vs indirect taxes - classification and base  [APPSC]

94.s: Which one of the following statements is correct regarding the general price effects of direct and indirect taxes?
o: Direct taxes are generally inflationary, whereas indirect taxes are generally non-inflationary
Direct taxes are generally non-inflationary, whereas indirect taxes are generally inflationary
Both direct and indirect taxes are invariably inflationary
Neither direct nor indirect taxes has any effect on prices
94.x: Direct taxes are generally considered non-inflationary, while indirect taxes can raise prices because their burden is incorporated into the prices of goods and services.
94.tq: Watch for the reversed-comparison trap between the two tax categories.
94.sec: Direct vs indirect taxes - classification and base  [APPSC]

94.s: Which one of the following is an indirect tax that has been largely subsumed in the Goods and Services Tax?
94.x: Service tax was an indirect tax on services and was subsumed in GST. Capital gains tax, STT and corporation tax are direct taxes.
94.tq: Separate the tax that entered GST from direct taxes that continue independently.
94.sec: Direct vs indirect taxes - classification and base  [APPSC]

94.s: Which one of the following is correctly classified as a group of taxes that generally yielded little revenue and came to be known as ‘paper taxes’?
o: Income tax, GST and customs duty
Wealth tax, gift tax and estate duty
Capital gains tax, STT and customs duty
Corporation tax, excise duty and service tax
94.x: Wealth tax, gift tax and estate duty are referred to as ‘paper taxes’ because they historically yielded little revenue. Wealth tax and estate duty were later abolished.
94.tq: Identify the distinctive group rather than treating every direct tax as a high-yield source.
94.sec: Direct vs indirect taxes - classification and base  [APPSC]

94.s: According to the Budget 2026–27 presentation of the Centre’s rupee, which is the largest single source of the Centre’s receipts?
94.x: Borrowings and other liabilities constitute 24% of the Centre’s rupee and are the largest overall source. Income tax is the largest individual tax source at 21%.
94.tq: Distinguish the largest overall receipt source from the largest tax source.
94.sec: Tax sources ranked in Centre's and States' revenue - direct vs indirect share  [APPSC]

94.s: In the Centre’s rupee for Budget 2026–27, the share of income tax is:
94.x: Income tax accounts for 21% of the Centre’s rupee in Budget 2026–27 and is the largest tax component. Borrowings account for 24% overall.
94.tq: Use ascending numerical options and distinguish adjacent receipt shares.
94.sec: Tax sources ranked in Centre's and States' revenue - direct vs indirect share  [APPSC]

94.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Centre’s rupee in Budget 2026–27:

1. Corporation tax accounts for 18%.
2. GST and other taxes account for 15%.
3. Union excise accounts for 6%.
4. Customs accounts for 4%.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
94.x: All four statements are correct: the respective shares are corporation tax 18%, GST and other taxes 15%, Union excise 6% and customs 4%.
94.tq: Read the receipt-share table carefully and test every numerical statement.
94.sec: Tax sources ranked in Centre's and States' revenue - direct vs indirect share  [APPSC]

94.s: The estimated net tax revenue of the Centre in Budget 2026–27 is:
94.x: The Budget Estimate for the Centre’s net tax revenue in 2026–27 is ₹28,72,135 crore, representing an increase of 8.0%. Non-tax revenue is estimated at ₹2,80,434 crore.
94.tq: Separate the net-tax figure from the nearby non-tax revenue figure and growth rate.
94.sec: Tax sources ranked in Centre's and States' revenue - direct vs indirect share  [APPSC]

94.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the changing composition of the Centre’s gross tax revenue?
o: Direct taxes now exceed indirect taxes, indicating a shift towards a more progressive structure
Direct taxes were abolished after the introduction of GST
Indirect taxes have always been higher than direct taxes
The share of direct taxes has steadily remained below 40% since the late 2000s
94.x: Indirect taxes dominated until the late 2000s, but direct taxes now exceed indirect taxes, reflecting a shift towards a more progressive tax structure.
94.tq: Identify the trend and reject absolute words such as ‘always’ and ‘abolished’.
94.sec: Tax sources ranked in Centre's and States' revenue - direct vs indirect share  [APPSC]

94.s: The share of direct taxes in the Centre’s gross tax revenue in FY 2025 was approximately:
94.x: Direct taxes constituted approximately 58.8% of the Centre’s gross tax revenue in FY 2025. The FY22–FY25 average was 55.5%, while the Budget Estimate for 2026–27 is 61.2%.
94.tq: Match each percentage with its specific year or period rather than using the nearest figure.
94.sec: Tax sources ranked in Centre's and States' revenue - direct vs indirect share  [APPSC]

94.s:
Which of the following statements regarding the Centre’s direct and indirect tax shares is correct?

1. Direct taxes accounted for 61.2% in the 2026–27 Budget Estimate.
2. Indirect taxes accounted for 38.8% in the 2026–27 Budget Estimate.
3. The average share of direct taxes during FY22–FY25 was 55.5%.

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
94.x: All three statements are correct. The 2026–27 Budget Estimate places direct taxes at 61.2% and indirect taxes at 38.8%, while the FY22–FY25 average direct-tax share was 55.5%.
94.tq: Combine the current estimate with the multi-year average and check whether all statements are supported.
94.sec: Tax sources ranked in Centre's and States' revenue - direct vs indirect share  [APPSC]

94.s: In Andhra Pradesh, the largest own-tax source in the revised estimate for 2024–25 is:
94.x: SGST is the largest own-tax source of Andhra Pradesh, yielding ₹36,296 crore or 38% of its own-tax revenue of ₹94,967 crore. State excise is the second-largest source.
94.tq: Distinguish a State’s own-tax source from its share in Union taxes.
94.sec: Tax sources ranked in Centre's and States' revenue - direct vs indirect share  [APPSC]

94.s: State excise constituted approximately what share of Andhra Pradesh’s own-tax revenue in the revised estimate for 2024–25?
94.x: State excise contributed ₹21,300 crore, which was approximately 22% of Andhra Pradesh’s own-tax revenue. It followed SGST, which contributed 38%.
94.tq: Link the percentage with the correct State revenue source instead of selecting the largest share.
94.sec: Tax sources ranked in Centre's and States' revenue - direct vs indirect share  [APPSC]

94.s: Which one of the following statements regarding business and profession tax is correct?
o: It is a customs levy imposed on imports by local bodies
It is a GST component collected exclusively by the Centre
It is a State levy under Article 276, subject to a ceiling of ₹2,500 per year
It is a Union levy under Article 280 with no statutory ceiling
94.x: Business and profession tax is a State levy under Article 276. Its constitutional ceiling is ₹2,500 per year, and it is not a Union source.
94.tq: Use the article-number and authority pair to catch the constitutional-provision trap.
94.sec: Tax sources ranked in Centre's and States' revenue - direct vs indirect share  [APPSC]

94.s:
Which of the following are included among Union taxes that are shared with the States on the advice of the Finance Commission?

1. Income tax on non-agricultural income
2. Corporation tax
3. Customs duty
4. Union excise duty
5. CGST and IGST
94.x: The listed Union taxes include non-agricultural income tax, corporation tax, customs, Union excise, CGST and IGST. Their sharing with States is associated with Finance Commission advice under the 80th Amendment, 2000, effective from 1 April 1996.
94.tq: Check the complete list of Union tax sources and avoid excluding customs merely because it is an indirect tax.
94.sec: Tax sources ranked in Centre's and States' revenue - direct vs indirect share  [APPSC]

94.s: The 80th Constitutional Amendment, 2000, relating to the sharing of Union taxes with the States, was effective from:
94.x: The 80th Amendment, enacted in 2000, operated retrospectively with effect from 1 April 1996 in relation to the sharing of Union tax revenues with the States.
94.tq: Separate the year of the constitutional amendment from its effective date.
94.sec: Tax sources ranked in Centre's and States' revenue - direct vs indirect share  [APPSC]

94.s:
Consider the following statements about the revenue receipts of States:

1. States’ own tax revenue formed about 50% of their revenue receipts in FY25.
2. The share in central taxes was the second-largest component at about 32% in FY25.
3. The CAG average for 2014–24 placed States’ own tax revenue at 47%.
4. The CAG average for 2014–24 placed grants at 17%.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
94.x: All four statements are correct. Own tax revenue was about 50% of State revenue receipts in FY25, the share in central taxes was about 32%, and the CAG average for 2014–24 was 47% for own tax revenue, 28% for tax share and 17% for grants.
94.tq: Keep the FY25 estimates separate from the CAG’s 2014–24 averages while checking each percentage.
94.sec: Tax sources ranked in Centre's and States' revenue - direct vs indirect share  [APPSC]

94.s: The tax-GDP ratio is calculated as:
o: Total tax revenue divided by nominal GDP
Total tax revenue divided by real GDP
Total non-tax revenue divided by nominal GDP
Nominal GDP divided by total tax revenue
94.x: The tax-GDP ratio is total tax revenue divided by nominal GDP. It is used as a yardstick of fiscal capacity.
94.tq: Use the exact numerator-denominator relationship in a formula-based question.
94.sec: Tax-GDP ratio - Centre, States, combined; falling ratio; peers | APPSC

94.s: A low tax-GDP ratio generally indicates:
o: High tax buoyancy in every year
A large informal sector or substantial tax evasion
A small informal sector and complete tax compliance
94.x: A low tax-GDP ratio may reflect a large informal sector or high tax evasion, thereby limiting fiscal capacity.
94.tq: Identify the fiscal implication rather than merely recalling the ratio formula.
94.sec: Tax-GDP ratio - Centre, States, combined; falling ratio; peers | APPSC

94.s:
Consider the following statements regarding India's tax-GDP ratio:
1. The World Bank regards 15 per cent as a tipping point for sustainable growth.
2. India's average tax-GDP ratio during 2001–2022 was 16.36 per cent.
3. India's average tax-GDP ratio during 2001–2022 was the highest among emerging and developing economies.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
94.x: The World Bank benchmark is 15 per cent, and India's 2001–2022 average was 16.36 per cent. It was the lowest, not the highest, among emerging and developing economies.
94.tq: Find the reversed comparison in the statement about India's position among peer economies.
94.sec: Tax-GDP ratio - Centre, States, combined; falling ratio; peers | APPSC

94.s: The gross tax revenue of the Centre was approximately what percentage of GDP in 2019–20?
94.x: The Centre's gross tax revenue was about 9.9 per cent of GDP in 2019–20.
94.tq: Distinguish the earlier reference-year figure from later tax-GDP estimates.
94.sec: Tax-GDP ratio - Centre, States, combined; falling ratio; peers | APPSC

94.s: The combined tax-GDP ratio of the Centre and the States was approximately:
94.x: The combined tax-GDP ratio of the Centre and States was approximately 19.6 per cent.
94.tq: Separate the combined Centre–State figure from the Centre-only and benchmark figures.
94.sec: Tax-GDP ratio - Centre, States, combined; falling ratio; peers | APPSC

94.s: The own tax revenue of States averages approximately what proportion of GSDP?
94.x: States' own tax revenue averages about 7 per cent of their Gross State Domestic Product.
94.tq: Match the level of government with its relevant denominator and percentage.
94.sec: Tax-GDP ratio - Centre, States, combined; falling ratio; peers | APPSC

94.s: A falling tax-GDP ratio, other things remaining unchanged, implies that:
o: Tax revenue is growing slower than GDP, weakening fiscal space and increasing borrowing requirements
Tax revenue is growing faster than GDP and fiscal space is expanding
Tax buoyancy is necessarily above one
94.x: A falling ratio indicates that tax revenue is growing more slowly than GDP. This weakens fiscal space and may lead to greater borrowing.
94.tq: Translate the direction of a ratio into its fiscal consequence.
94.sec: Tax-GDP ratio - Centre, States, combined; falling ratio; peers | APPSC

94.s: Tax buoyancy is defined as:
o: Percentage change in GDP divided by percentage change in tax revenue
Change in direct taxes divided by change in indirect taxes
Tax revenue divided by nominal GDP
Percentage change in tax revenue divided by percentage change in GDP
94.x: Tax buoyancy equals the percentage change in tax revenue divided by the percentage change in GDP. A value above one means tax revenue grows faster than GDP.
94.tq: Distinguish tax buoyancy from the tax-GDP ratio by comparing their formulas.
94.sec: Tax-GDP ratio - Centre, States, combined; falling ratio; peers | APPSC

94.s: In the 2026–27 Budget Estimates, the Centre's gross tax buoyancy and its direct-tax and indirect-tax components were respectively estimated at:
94.x: The estimated gross tax buoyancy was 0.8, comprising direct-tax buoyancy of 1.1 and indirect-tax buoyancy of 0.3.
94.tq: Preserve the order of an aggregate figure followed by its components.
94.sec: Tax-GDP ratio - Centre, States, combined; falling ratio; peers | APPSC

94.s: Which one of the following correctly describes a tax?
o: A temporary levy retained only until a specified purpose is achieved
A compulsory contribution imposed under legal authority without a direct quid pro quo
A voluntary payment made for a specific government service
An additional percentage charge imposed only on an existing tax
94.x: A tax is a compulsory pecuniary contribution imposed under the authority of law to finance government, without a direct quid pro quo.
94.tq: Discriminate the general category of tax from fee, cess and surcharge.
94.sec: Tax, cess, surcharge and fee - distinction [APPSC]

94.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
o: Fee — payment for a specific service involving quid pro quo
Cess — additional charge on tax payable, usually permanent
Surcharge — tax on tax for a specific purpose that ends when the purpose is met
Tax — payment made only when a specific service is received
94.x: A fee is paid for a specific service and involves quid pro quo. A cess is a tax on tax for a specific purpose, while a surcharge is an additional charge on tax payable.
94.tq: Use the exact meaning of each closely related levy to eliminate swapped definitions.
94.sec: Tax, cess, surcharge and fee - distinction [APPSC]

94.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. A cess is imposed for a specific purpose and normally ends when that purpose is achieved.
2. A surcharge is an additional charge on the tax payable.
3. A surcharge is payable even when no tax is due.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
94.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. No surcharge is payable when there is no tax due, so statement 3 is false.
94.tq: Spot the absolute reversal in the statement concerning the liability for surcharge.
94.sec: Tax, cess, surcharge and fee - distinction [APPSC]

94.s: Under Article 271 of the Constitution, surcharge proceeds are treated as follows:
o: They are compulsorily shared with States through the divisible pool
They are collected only by States
They are transferred exclusively to local bodies
They are retained by the Centre and are not shared with States
94.x: Surcharges under Article 271 are retained by the Centre and are not shared with States. Cesses are also outside the divisible pool.
94.tq: Recall the constitutional treatment of a specific revenue instrument.
94.sec: Tax, cess, surcharge and fee - distinction [APPSC]

94.s: The Clean Energy Cess imposed on coal under the Finance Act, 2010 was renamed as:
94.x: The Clean Energy Cess on coal, introduced under the Finance Act, 2010, was renamed the Clean Environment Cess in Budget 2016–17.
94.tq: Apply the renamed-levy trap by linking the original name, base and later name.
94.sec: Tax, cess, surcharge and fee - distinction [APPSC]

94.s: The Chelliah approach to tax reform primarily favours:
o: Abolition of all tax exemptions without widening the base
Higher tax rates with a narrow base
Lower tax rates with a broader tax base
94.x: The Chelliah approach favours base widening through more taxpayers and fewer exemptions, together with lower rates rather than rate hikes.
94.tq: Identify the reform principle expressed through the rates-versus-base comparison.
94.sec: Tax, cess, surcharge and fee - distinction [APPSC]

94.s: Which of the following correctly represents the relationship among personal income, personal disposable income and taxes?
o: Personal disposable income equals personal income minus personal direct taxes and non-tax payments
Personal disposable income equals national income minus corporate tax only
Personal disposable income excludes transfer payments and government interest receipts by definition
Personal disposable income equals personal income plus personal taxes and non-tax payments
94.x: Personal disposable income is personal income less personal direct taxes and non-tax payments.
94.tq: Use the subtraction structure to distinguish personal income from disposable income.
94.sec: Tax concepts in national income - disposable income, demand, productivity [APPSC]

94.s:
Consider the following items:
1. Undistributed profits
2. Social security contributions
3. Corporate tax
4. Transfer payments
5. Net interest paid by the government
Which of the above are adjustments used in deriving Personal Income from National Income?
94.x: Personal Income is derived as National Income minus undistributed profits, social security contributions and corporate tax, plus transfer payments and net interest paid by the government.
94.tq: Track both deductions and additions in a national-income identity.
94.sec: Tax concepts in national income - disposable income, demand, productivity [APPSC]

94.s: A reduction in direct taxes is most likely to produce which immediate effect, other things remaining equal?
o: Lower disposable income and lower consumption demand
Lower disposable income but higher tax buoyancy by definition
Higher disposable income and higher consumption demand
94.x: A cut in direct taxes raises disposable income, which can increase consumption demand. It may also support savings and investment.
94.tq: Follow the causal chain from a tax change to disposable income and demand.
94.sec: Tax concepts in national income - disposable income, demand, productivity [APPSC]

94.s:
Assertion (A): The Laffer curve is represented as an inverted-U curve.
Reason (R): Tax revenue is zero at both a zero tax rate and a 100 per cent tax rate.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
94.x: Both statements are correct. Revenue is zero at the two extreme rates in the model, producing the inverted-U relationship between tax rates and revenue.
94.tq: Test whether the reason explains the shape asserted, not merely whether both statements are true.
94.sec: Tax concepts in national income - disposable income, demand, productivity [APPSC]

94.s: The Laffer curve was popularised by Arthur Laffer, while the term was coined by:
94.x: Arthur Laffer popularised the Laffer curve in 1974, and the term was coined by Jude Wanniski.
