Central assistance for Union Territory Plans
102.x: Interest payments formed part of the larger non-Plan expenditure category. Central Plans and central assistance for State and Union Territory Plans were Plan expenditure.
102.tq: Use the direct association between interest payments and the former non-Plan category.
102.sec: Plan vs non-plan expenditure - items and end of the classification  [APPSC]

102.s: Which of the following sets contains only items classified as non-Plan expenditure under the former system?
o: Interest payments, defence, subsidies, salaries and pensions
Central Plans, defence, subsidies, salaries and pensions
Central assistance for State Plans, pensions, salaries and interest payments
Central Plans, Central assistance for Union Territory Plans and defence
102.x: Interest payments, defence, subsidies, salaries, pensions and maintenance of assets created in earlier Plans were non-Plan items. Central Plans and central assistance for State or Union Territory Plans were Plan items.
102.tq: Check every item in a set against the former classification rather than identifying only one familiar item.
102.sec: Plan vs non-plan expenditure - items and end of the classification  [APPSC]

102.s: The classification of expenditure into Plan and non-Plan was discontinued from which Budget year?
102.x: The Plan and non-Plan classification ended from Budget 2017-18 on the recommendation of the Expenditure Management Commission.
102.tq: Distinguish the discontinuation year from adjacent Budget years.
102.sec: Plan vs non-plan expenditure - items and end of the classification  [APPSC]

102.s: The Plan and non-Plan classification was replaced primarily by which classification?
102.x: After the discontinuation of Plan and non-Plan expenditure, the revenue-capital classification became the principal framework.
102.tq: Discriminate between two different expenditure classifications that are commonly interchanged.
102.sec: Plan vs non-plan expenditure - items and end of the classification  [APPSC]

102.s: Which of the following statements about the Union Budget changes associated with the end of Plan and non-Plan classification is correct?
o: The Railway Budget was abolished and the Budget was presented on 15 August.
The Railway Budget was merged with the Union Budget and the Budget was presented on 31 March.
The Railway Budget was separated and the Budget was presented on 1 April.
The Railway Budget was merged with the Union Budget and the Budget was presented on 1 February.
102.x: The relevant Budget changes included the merger of the Railway Budget with the Union Budget and presentation of the Union Budget on 1 February.
102.tq: Pair the two associated procedural changes instead of selecting only one of them.
102.sec: Plan vs non-plan expenditure - items and end of the classification  [APPSC]

102.s:
Match List-I with List-II regarding developmental and non-developmental expenditure:
List-I (Category)
 a. Developmental expenditure
 b. Non-developmental expenditure
 c. Economic and social services
 d. Routine operational spending
List-II (Description)
 i. Defence, interest payments and pensions
 ii. Education, health, irrigation and agriculture
 iii. A component of developmental expenditure
 iv. Consumptive expenditure required for routine operations
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
102.x: Developmental expenditure includes education, health, irrigation and agriculture; non-developmental expenditure includes defence, interest payments and pensions. Economic and social services are developmental, while routine operational spending is consumptive.
102.tq: Start with the sure pair linking education and health to developmental expenditure.
102.sec: Developmental vs non-developmental expenditure - classifying items  [APPSC]

102.s: Which one of the following is NOT generally classified as developmental expenditure?
102.x: Defence is classified as non-developmental expenditure. Rural development, social welfare and public health are developmental activities.
102.tq: Find the item outside the growth and quality-of-life group.
102.sec: Developmental vs non-developmental expenditure - classifying items  [APPSC]

102.s:
Consider the following statements regarding developmental expenditure:
1. It includes expenditure on education and health.
2. It includes expenditure on employment and rural development.
3. It is intended to stimulate growth, employment and quality of life.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
102.x: All three statements correctly describe developmental expenditure and its principal objectives.
102.tq: Recognise that the functional list and the stated economic purpose belong to the same category.
102.sec: Developmental vs non-developmental expenditure - classifying items  [APPSC]

102.s: Which one of the following combinations consists entirely of non-developmental expenditure items?
o: Interest payments, police and law and order, tax-collection charges
Employment, rural development and public health
102.x: Interest payments, police and law and order, tax-collection charges and administrative expenditure are non-developmental items.
102.tq: Classify the entire combination, not merely the first item.
102.sec: Developmental vs non-developmental expenditure - classifying items  [APPSC]

102.s:
Assertion (A): Developmental expenditure is associated with improvement in employment and quality of life.
Reason (R): It includes economic and social services such as education, health, irrigation and rural development.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
102.x: Both statements are true, and the inclusion of economic and social services explains why developmental expenditure improves employment and quality of life.
102.tq: Test whether the functional examples in the Reason explain the stated outcome in the Assertion.
102.sec: Developmental vs non-developmental expenditure - classifying items  [APPSC]

102.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched with the revenue-capital classification?
o: Maintenance of existing assets — Capital expenditure
Loans and advances to States — Capital expenditure
102.x: Loans and advances to States are capital expenditure because they affect the Government's financial assets. Maintenance of existing assets and interest payments are revenue expenditure, while repayment of loans reduces liabilities and is capital expenditure.
102.tq: Use the effect on assets or liabilities to identify the correct classification.
102.sec: Revenue vs capital expenditure - classifying items  [APPSC]

102.s: A government expenditure creates a new asset or reduces an existing liability. Under the revenue-capital distinction, it is ordinarily treated as:
102.x: Capital expenditure either creates assets or reduces liabilities. Revenue expenditure generally neither creates an asset nor reduces a liability.
102.tq: Apply the asset-liability test instead of relying on the department incurring the expenditure.
102.sec: Revenue vs capital expenditure - classifying items  [APPSC]

102.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Grants to State governments remain revenue expenditure even if the States use them to create assets.
2. Purchase of defence equipment can be capital outlay.
3. Subsidies are ordinarily classified as capital expenditure because they support production.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
102.x: Grants to State governments are revenue expenditure even when they create assets for the States, and defence equipment can be capital outlay. Subsidies are revenue expenditure, not capital expenditure.
102.tq: Identify the exception concerning grants and reject the reversed treatment of subsidies.
102.sec: Revenue vs capital expenditure - classifying items  [APPSC]

102.s: Which of the following is correctly classified as revenue expenditure?
o: Loan advanced to a public sector undertaking
102.x: Maintenance of existing assets is revenue expenditure. Construction of an airport, repayment of loans and loans to public sector undertakings are capital expenditure.
102.tq: Distinguish ordinary maintenance from expenditure that creates assets or reduces liabilities.
102.sec: Revenue vs capital expenditure - classifying items  [APPSC]

102.s: Which of the following is an example of an implicit or hidden subsidy?
o: A fertiliser subsidy shown in the Budget
An export incentive shown as a Budget provision
A food subsidy shown as a separate Budget line item
Under-pricing of higher education in a public university
102.x: Under-pricing of publicly provided services, such as higher education in public universities, is an implicit or hidden subsidy. Food, fertiliser and export incentives shown in the Budget are explicit subsidies.
102.tq: Distinguish a visible Budget line item from under-pricing of a publicly provided service.
102.sec: Subsidies - major heads, explicit vs hidden, NBS, Oil Pool Account  [APPSC]

102.s: Which of the following sets contains only explicit subsidies?
o: Food, fertiliser, LPG and interest subvention
Public university education, irrigation water and public health
Irrigation water, LPG and higher education
102.x: Food, fertiliser, LPG, export incentives and interest subvention are explicit subsidies because they are shown as Budget line items. The other listed services are examples of hidden subsidies when under-priced.
102.tq: Use the visibility-in-the-Budget test to separate explicit from hidden subsidies.
102.sec: Subsidies - major heads, explicit vs hidden, NBS, Oil Pool Account  [APPSC]

102.s: Under the Nutrient Based Subsidy scheme, subsidy is fixed with reference to:
o: The quantity of food grains procured by the Government
The quantity of specified nutrients in decontrolled P&K fertilisers
The retail price of urea alone
The international price of crude oil
102.x: NBS fixes subsidy per kilogram of nutrient in decontrolled phosphorus- and potassium-based fertilisers. Urea is outside the NBS framework.
102.tq: Link the scheme name to its nutrient-based calculation rather than to the price of a single fertiliser.
102.sec: Subsidies - major heads, explicit vs hidden, NBS, Oil Pool Account  [APPSC]

102.s: The Nutrient Based Subsidy scheme was introduced from:
102.x: The Nutrient Based Subsidy scheme commenced on 1 April 2010.
102.tq: Discriminate the notified commencement date from adjacent years.
102.sec: Subsidies - major heads, explicit vs hidden, NBS, Oil Pool Account  [APPSC]

102.s: Which one of the following statements regarding the Nutrient Based Subsidy scheme is correct?
o: It covers only urea and excludes all P&K fertilisers.
It covers 22 grades, including DAP, MOP and SSP, while urea remains outside it.
It applies only to one grade of fertiliser and fixes subsidy per tonne of crude oil.
It covers all fertilisers, including urea, without reference to nutrient content.
102.x: NBS covers 22 grades of decontrolled P&K fertilisers, including DAP, MOP and SSP, and fixes subsidy per kilogram of N, P, K and S nutrients. Urea is outside the scheme.
102.tq: Separate the covered P&K grades and nutrients from the excluded fertiliser, urea.
102.sec: Subsidies - major heads, explicit vs hidden, NBS, Oil Pool Account  [APPSC]

102.s: The Oil Pool Account associated with the Administered Price Mechanism was dismantled in:
102.x: The Oil Pool Account under the Administered Price Mechanism was dismantled in April 2002.
102.tq: Use the precise month-year combination to avoid confusing the reform with neighbouring years.
102.sec: Subsidies - major heads, explicit vs hidden, NBS, Oil Pool Account  [APPSC]

102.s: After the dismantling of the Oil Pool Account, later under-recoveries of oil companies were compensated through:
102.x: Later petroleum under-recoveries were compensated through oil bonds.
102.tq: Match the petroleum under-recovery mechanism with its specific compensation instrument.
102.sec: Subsidies - major heads, explicit vs hidden, NBS, Oil Pool Account  [APPSC]

102.s:
Which of the following principles was associated with the approach of the Sixteenth Finance Commission towards subsidies?
1. Retaining only well-targeted subsidies
2. Providing exclusion criteria and sunset clauses
3. Permitting off-budget financing of subsidies without restriction
Which of the statements given above are correct?
102.x: The approach supports well-targeted subsidies, exclusion criteria and sunset clauses. It does not support unrestricted off-budget financing of subsidies.
102.tq: Identify the negative statement that reverses the Commission's transparency and targeting principles.
102.sec: Subsidies - major heads, explicit vs hidden, NBS, Oil Pool Account  [APPSC]

102.s: In Budget 2026-27, the total subsidy provision was approximately:
102.x: The total subsidy provision in Budget 2026-27 was ₹4,54,773 crore, representing a 3.1 per cent decline from the 2025-26 revised estimate.
102.tq: Read the exact Budget figure and distinguish it from closely spaced alternatives.
102.sec: Subsidies - major heads, explicit vs hidden, NBS, Oil Pool Account  [APPSC]

102.s: In Budget 2026-27, food and fertiliser subsidies together accounted for approximately what share of the total subsidy bill?
102.x: Food subsidy of ₹2,27,629 crore and fertiliser subsidy of ₹1,70,799 crore together accounted for 87 per cent of the total subsidy bill.
102.tq: Combine the two stated major heads and compare their aggregate share with the total bill.
102.sec: Subsidies - major heads, explicit vs hidden, NBS, Oil Pool Account  [APPSC]

102.s: The major subsidies comprising food, fertiliser and petroleum in Budget 2026-27 were estimated at approximately what share of GDP?
102.x: Food, fertiliser and petroleum subsidies together amounted to about ₹4.11 lakh crore, equivalent to 1.0 per cent of GDP.
102.tq: Match the aggregate subsidy amount with its stated GDP ratio.
102.sec: Subsidies - major heads, explicit vs hidden, NBS, Oil Pool Account  [APPSC]

102.s: The Centre plus States public expenditure to GDP ratio was approximately what in the Economic Survey 2016-17?
102.x: Public expenditure of the Centre and States together was about 28 per cent of GDP in the Economic Survey 2016-17.
102.tq: Identify the combined-government ratio rather than a Union-only expenditure ratio.
102.sec: Public expenditure trends - expenditure-GDP ratio, largest items, committed expenditure  [APPSC]

102.s: According to Union Budget Estimates 2026-27, total expenditure was approximately:
102.x: The Union Budget Estimates 2026-27 placed total expenditure at ₹53,47,315 crore, or 13.6 per cent of GDP.
102.tq: Use the exact total expenditure figure and avoid confusing it with the revenue or capital components.
102.sec: Public expenditure trends - expenditure-GDP ratio, largest items, committed expenditure  [APPSC]

102.s: Which of the following correctly represents the Union Budget Estimates 2026-27?
o: Revenue expenditure 3.1% of GDP and capital expenditure 10.5% of GDP
Revenue expenditure 7.7% of GDP and capital expenditure 13.6% of GDP
Revenue expenditure 13.6% of GDP and capital expenditure 10.5% of GDP
Revenue expenditure 10.5% of GDP and capital expenditure 3.1% of GDP
102.x: Revenue expenditure was estimated at ₹41.25 lakh crore, or 10.5 per cent of GDP, while capital expenditure was ₹12.22 lakh crore, or 3.1 per cent of GDP.
102.tq: Keep the revenue and capital ratios paired with their correct expenditure heads.
102.sec: Public expenditure trends - expenditure-GDP ratio, largest items, committed expenditure  [APPSC]

102.s: In the 2026-27 Union Budget expenditure composition, the largest share was assigned to:
102.x: States' share of taxes accounted for 22 per cent of the expenditure composition, followed by interest at 20 per cent and central sector schemes at 17 per cent.
102.tq: Read the expenditure composition chart as a ranking question rather than relying on the usual generic largest-item answer.
102.sec: Public expenditure trends - expenditure-GDP ratio, largest items, committed expenditure  [APPSC]

102.s:
Arrange the following components of Union Budget 2026-27 expenditure in descending order of their stated shares:
A. Defence
B. Central Sector Schemes
C. Interest
D. States' share of taxes
102.x: The shares were States' share of taxes 22 per cent, interest 20 per cent, Central Sector Schemes 17 per cent and defence 11 per cent.
102.tq: Rank the options by the numerical shares, starting with the largest component.
102.sec: Public expenditure trends - expenditure-GDP ratio, largest items, committed expenditure  [APPSC]

102.s: Interest payments in Union Budget Estimates 2026-27 were approximately what proportion of total expenditure and revenue receipts, respectively?
102.x: Interest payments of ₹14,03,972 crore represented 26 per cent of total expenditure and 40 per cent of revenue receipts.
102.tq: Do not reverse the two denominators when comparing the percentages.
102.sec: Public expenditure trends - expenditure-GDP ratio, largest items, committed expenditure  [APPSC]

102.s: Which of the following correctly describes the trend in interest payments as a share of revenue receipts?
102.x: Interest payments were 37 per cent of revenue receipts in 2013-14, 42 per cent in 2020-21 and 40 per cent in the 2026-27 estimate.
102.tq: Preserve the year-wise order while comparing closely related percentages.
102.sec: Public expenditure trends - expenditure-GDP ratio, largest items, committed expenditure  [APPSC]

102.s: Committed expenditure consisting of salaries, pensions and interest payments accounted for what proportion of revenue receipts?
102.x: Committed expenditure, comprising salaries, pensions and interest payments, was 65.3 per cent of revenue receipts.
102.tq: Associate the exact percentage with the complete committed-expenditure group.
102.sec: Public expenditure trends - expenditure-GDP ratio, largest items, committed expenditure  [APPSC]

102.s: Which statement correctly represents the trend in Union revenue expenditure as a percentage of GDP?
o: It declined from 13.6% in FY22 to 3.1% in FY25.
It declined from 13.6% in FY22 to 10.9% in FY25.
It remained unchanged at 13.6% between FY22 and FY25.
It increased from 10.9% in FY22 to 13.6% in FY25.
102.x: Revenue expenditure declined from 13.6 per cent of GDP in FY22 to 10.9 per cent in FY25.
102.tq: Check both the direction of change and the correct years before selecting the trend.
102.sec: Public expenditure trends - expenditure-GDP ratio, largest items, committed expenditure  [APPSC]

102.s: The share of revenue expenditure in total Union expenditure changed from 2014-15 to the 2026-27 Budget Estimate as follows:
102.x: Revenue expenditure accounted for 88 per cent of total expenditure in 2014-15 and about 77 per cent in the 2026-27 Budget Estimate.
102.tq: Identify the direction of the long-term share change rather than confusing it with the committed-expenditure ratio.
102.sec: Public expenditure trends - expenditure-GDP ratio, largest items, committed expenditure  [APPSC]

102.s:
Which of the following statements regarding State government expenditure is correct?
1. States' spending was between 16.15 per cent and 17.49 per cent of GSDP during 2014-24.
2. Revenue expenditure constituted 80-87 per cent of total expenditure.
3. Committed expenditure plus subsidies constituted 51.76 per cent of revenue expenditure in FY24.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
102.x: All three statements correctly describe the stated expenditure pattern of States: spending of 16.15-17.49 per cent of GSDP, revenue expenditure of 80-87 per cent of total expenditure, and 51.76 per cent for committed expenditure plus subsidies in FY24.
102.tq: Verify each numerical range and the specific FY24 percentage before choosing the combined code.
102.sec: Public expenditure trends - expenditure-GDP ratio, largest items, committed expenditure  [APPSC]

102.s: State government total expenditure as a percentage of GDP changed from FY19 to FY24 in which manner?
102.x: Total expenditure of States declined from 15.7 per cent of GDP in FY19 to 15.4 per cent in FY24.
102.tq: Compare the two specified years and retain the correct direction of movement.
102.sec: Public expenditure trends - expenditure-GDP ratio, largest items, committed expenditure  [APPSC]

102.s: Which of the following correctly defines effective capital expenditure?
o: Capital expenditure plus grants-in-aid for creation of capital assets
Revenue expenditure plus loans to State Governments
Capital expenditure minus grants-in-aid for creation of capital assets
Capital outlay plus interest payments on public debt
102.x: Effective capital expenditure is calculated as capital expenditure plus grants-in-aid for the creation of capital assets.
102.tq: Test the exact formula by distinguishing additions from deductions.
102.sec: Capital expenditure push - effective capex, special assistance to States

102.s: The effective capital expenditure provided for in BE 2026-27 is approximately:
102.x: Effective capital expenditure in BE 2026-27 is ₹17.15 lakh crore.
102.tq: Use the precise budget figure rather than the related capital-outlay amount.
102.sec: Capital expenditure push - effective capex, special assistance to States

102.s: What percentage of GDP does the effective capital expenditure of ₹17.15 lakh crore represent in BE 2026-27?
102.x: The effective capital expenditure is estimated at 4.4 per cent of GDP in BE 2026-27.
102.tq: Separate the expenditure amount from its GDP ratio.
102.sec: Capital expenditure push - effective capex, special assistance to States

102.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Grants-in-aid for creation of capital assets account for ₹4.93 lakh crore of effective capital expenditure in BE 2026-27.
2. Effective capital expenditure is estimated to be 101.1 per cent of the fiscal deficit.
3. Effective capital expenditure excludes grants-in-aid for creation of capital assets.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
102.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because effective capital expenditure includes such grants-in-aid.
102.tq: Find the statement that reverses the stated definition and test the two linked numerical facts.
102.sec: Capital expenditure push - effective capex, special assistance to States

102.s:
With reference to capital expenditure in the Union Budget, consider the following statements:
1. Capital expenditure is ₹12,21,821 crore.
2. Capital outlay forms the larger component of this capital expenditure.
3. Loans account for ₹2,78,780 crore of the capital expenditure.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
102.x: All three statements are correct. Capital expenditure of ₹12,21,821 crore comprises capital outlay of ₹9,43,042 crore and loans of ₹2,78,780 crore.
102.tq: Split the aggregate into its two components before selecting the coded option.
102.sec: Capital expenditure push - effective capex, special assistance to States

102.s: Which of the following correctly represents the reported growth in capital expenditure during the periods mentioned?
o: 28 per cent in April-November 2025 and 11.5 per cent in Q1 2026-27
28 per cent in April-November 2025 and 23.7 per cent in Q1 2026-27
23.7 per cent in April-November 2025 and 28 per cent in Q1 2026-27
11.5 per cent in April-November 2025 and 28 per cent in Q1 2026-27
102.x: Capital expenditure grew by 28 per cent during April-November 2025 and by 23.7 per cent in Q1 2026-27.
102.tq: Match each growth rate with its correct time period instead of comparing the figures alone.
102.sec: Capital expenditure push - effective capex, special assistance to States

102.s: The Special Assistance to States for Capital Investment (SASCI) provides States with:
102.x: SASCI provides 50-year interest-free loans to States for capital expenditure.
102.tq: Use the application-purpose and loan-terms pair to distinguish the scheme from ordinary grants.
102.sec: Capital expenditure push - effective capex, special assistance to States

102.s: The allocation under SASCI for 2026-27 is:
102.x: The allocation under SASCI for 2026-27 is ₹1.85 lakh crore.
102.tq: Distinguish the scheme allocation from the Union’s aggregate capital-expenditure figures.
102.sec: Capital expenditure push - effective capex, special assistance to States

102.s: The fiscal multiplier of capital expenditure in India has been estimated at:
102.x: The fiscal multiplier of capital expenditure in India is estimated at 2.5-3.
102.tq: Identify the stated range rather than selecting a familiar but lower multiplier range.
102.sec: Capital expenditure push - effective capex, special assistance to States

102.s:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer.

List-I (Body)
a. Expenditure Reforms Commission
b. Expenditure Management Commission

List-II (Year and Chairperson)
i. 2000 - K.P. Geethakrishnan
ii. 2014 - Bimal Jalan
iii. 2000 - Bimal Jalan
iv. 2014 - K.P. Geethakrishnan
102.x: The Expenditure Reforms Commission was constituted in February 2000 under K.P. Geethakrishnan, while the Expenditure Management Commission was associated with 2014 and chaired by Bimal Jalan.
102.tq: Start from the sure chairperson-year pair and eliminate the swapped combinations.
102.sec: Expenditure reform bodies - chairpersons

102.s: The Expenditure Reforms Commission, constituted in February 2000, was chaired by:
102.x: The chairperson was K.P. Geethakrishnan. The initials are sometimes incorrectly written as K.R.; the correct initials are K.P.
102.tq: Discriminate between closely similar initials in a proper name.
102.sec: Expenditure reform bodies - chairpersons

102.s: Which one of the following statements is correct regarding Bimal Jalan in the context of expenditure-related reform bodies?
o: He chaired the Expenditure Reforms Commission in February 2000.
He chaired the Peacock-Wiseman Committee in the United Kingdom in 1961.
He chaired the Expenditure Management Commission associated with 2014.
He formulated Wagner’s law in the nineteenth century.
102.x: Bimal Jalan chaired the Expenditure Management Commission associated with 2014. He should not be confused with K.P. Geethakrishnan, who chaired the Expenditure Reforms Commission.
102.tq: Use the wrong-person-for-the-deed trap to separate two chairpersons.
102.sec: Expenditure reform bodies - chairpersons

102.s: Wagner’s law states that, as an economy industrialises:
o: Public expenditure rises faster than national income
Public expenditure falls faster than national income
Public expenditure rises only during wars and crises
Public expenditure remains constant irrespective of national income
102.x: Wagner’s law, also called the law of increasing state activity, holds that public expenditure rises faster than national income as an economy industrialises.
102.tq: Match the law with its distinctive continuous income-related trend.
102.sec: Wagner's law and Peacock-Wiseman hypothesis

102.s: Which of the following best describes the Peacock-Wiseman hypothesis?
o: Public expenditure rises in steps, particularly during wars and crises, and generally does not return to its earlier level.
Public expenditure declines whenever the tolerable tax burden increases.
Public expenditure rises continuously and smoothly with national income.
Public expenditure is unrelated to taxation and national emergencies.
102.x: The Peacock-Wiseman hypothesis, based on UK data and associated with 1961, states that public spending rises in steps during wars and crises and does not fully fall back afterwards.
102.tq: Identify the stepwise pattern and the lasting effect rather than Wagner’s continuous-rise formulation.
102.sec: Wagner's law and Peacock-Wiseman hypothesis

102.s: The displacement effect in public expenditure theory is associated with:
o: The fiscal multiplier of capital expenditure
102.x: The displacement effect is associated with the Peacock-Wiseman hypothesis. Wars and crises raise the tolerable tax burden and displace public spending to a higher level.
102.tq: Discriminate between the two theories using their signature concepts.
102.sec: Wagner's law and Peacock-Wiseman hypothesis

102.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes Wagner’s law from the Peacock-Wiseman hypothesis?
o: Wagner’s law concerns continuous growth of public expenditure with industrialisation, whereas Peacock-Wiseman concerns stepwise increases caused by wars and crises.
Wagner’s law concerns stepwise spending after crises, whereas Peacock-Wiseman concerns continuous growth with income.
Both theories state that public expenditure falls after a crisis.
Both theories are concerned exclusively with subsidy expenditure.
102.x: Wagner’s law links the continuous rise of public expenditure with industrialisation and income, whereas Peacock-Wiseman explains discontinuous increases through crises and the displacement effect.
102.tq: Place the two similar theories side by side and identify their defining contrast.
102.sec: Wagner's law and Peacock-Wiseman hypothesis

102.s: The Golden Rule in the context of public finance emphasises that government borrowing should ordinarily be used for:
o: Payment of all routine salaries and pensions
Creation of assets through capital expenditure
Financing every form of revenue expenditure
102.x: The Golden Rule emphasises borrowing only for asset creation, making the quality and composition of spending more important than its size alone.
102.tq: Apply the rule to distinguish asset-creating expenditure from routine revenue expenditure.
102.sec: Universal angles

102.s: Which of the following current developments is associated with subsidy expenditure in 2026-27?
o: A crude-oil-driven subsidy overshoot of about ₹50,000 crore
A complete elimination of petroleum-related subsidies
A fertilizer-subsidy reduction of exactly ₹50,000 crore
A crude-oil-driven subsidy undershoot of about ₹50,000 crore
102.x: A crude-oil-driven subsidy overshoot of about ₹50,000 crore was considered likely in 2026-27.
102.tq: Watch the direction of change and the approximate amount in a current-affairs figure.
102.sec: Universal angles

102.s: According to the stated 2026-27 position, how many of the 18 large States were expected to budget revenue deficits?
102.x: Nine of the 18 large States budgeted revenue deficits for 2026-27.
102.tq: Convert the fraction-like current-affairs statement into an exact count.
102.sec: Universal angles

102.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Andhra Pradesh’s revised estimates for 2025-26:
1. Revenue expenditure was ₹2,38,022 crore.
2. Capital outlay was ₹33,135 crore.
3. Capital outlay was more than double the 2024-25 figure of ₹16,141 crore.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
102.x: All three statements are correct for Andhra Pradesh’s 2025-26 revised estimates. Capital outlay of ₹33,135 crore was more than double ₹16,141 crore in 2024-25.
102.tq: Check the two expenditure figures and then verify the comparison with the earlier year.
102.sec: Universal angles

102.s: In Andhra Pradesh, the capital outlay provided in BE 2026-27 was:
102.x: Andhra Pradesh’s BE 2026-27 capital outlay was ₹48,698 crore, representing a 47 per cent increase.
102.tq: Distinguish the latest budget estimate from the preceding revised-estimate figure.
102.sec: Universal angles

102.s: Which of the following statements regarding Andhra Pradesh’s committed expenditure is correct?
o: Committed spending accounts for 75.3 per cent of revenue receipts and consists exclusively of capital outlay.
Committed spending accounts for 55.3 per cent of revenue receipts and eliminates revenue expenditure.
Committed spending accounts for 45.3 per cent of revenue receipts and leaves ample room for capex.
Committed spending accounts for 65.3 per cent of revenue receipts and leaves little room for additional spending flexibility.
102.x: Committed spending accounts for 65.3 per cent of Andhra Pradesh’s revenue receipts, leaving little room for fiscal flexibility. The CAG flagged rising committed expenditure and weak capital expenditure in the State.
102.tq: Use the percentage and its fiscal implication together to reject reversed or exaggerated claims.
102.sec: Universal angles

103.s: Under Article 292 of the Constitution, Public Debt of the Union comprises borrowings contracted against the:
103.x: Article 292 relates to borrowings by the Government of India against the security of the Consolidated Fund of India. Other liabilities are recorded in the Public Account.
103.tq: Recall the constitutional article associated with the borrowing authority.
103.sec: Centre's liabilities - internal debt, other liabilities, external debt  [APPSC]

103.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched with the classification of the Union Government's liabilities?
o: Loans from foreign governments — Internal debt
103.x: Small savings and post-office deposits are other liabilities recorded in the Public Account. Market loans are internal debt, while loans from foreign governments are external debt.
103.tq: Distinguish internal debt, other liabilities and external debt by identifying the correct category.

103.s: Which of the following is included among the marketable components of the internal debt of the Union Government?

103.tq: Use category-based elimination among closely related government liabilities.
103.sec: Centre's liabilities - internal debt, other liabilities, external debt  [APPSC]

103.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the liabilities of the Central Government:
1. G-Secs constitute more than 90% of Central Government debt.
2. Internal debt constitutes 96.7% of public debt.
3. External liabilities constitute 3.3% of the Centre's total liabilities.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
103.x: All three statements are correct: G-Secs account for over 90% of Central Government debt, internal debt forms 96.7% of public debt, and external liabilities form 3.3% of total Centre liabilities.
103.tq: Test several percentages belonging to the same liability classification.
103.sec: Centre's liabilities - internal debt, other liabilities, external debt  [APPSC]

103.s: The outstanding liabilities of the Central Government in Budget Estimates 2026-27 were estimated at approximately:
103.x: The Centre's outstanding liabilities in BE 2026-27 were estimated at ₹2,14,82,050 crore, or 55.6% of GDP.
103.tq: Separate the complete figure from truncated or differently scaled numerical distractors.
103.sec: Centre's liabilities - internal debt, other liabilities, external debt  [APPSC]

103.s: Market borrowings are regarded as the:

103.sec: Market borrowings - share in capital receipts; household savings and government borrowing  [APPSC]

103.s: In 2026-27, ‘Borrowings and other liabilities’ accounted for approximately how much of every rupee of government receipts?
103.x: Borrowings and other liabilities were estimated to account for 24 paise of every rupee in 2026-27 and formed the single largest receipt head.
103.tq: Recall the precise share and reject nearby altered percentages.
103.sec: Market borrowings - share in capital receipts; household savings and government borrowing  [APPSC]

103.s: Which one of the following correctly represents the 2026-27 gross and net market borrowings through dated securities?
o: Gross ₹11.73 lakh crore; net ₹17.20 lakh crore
Gross ₹19.03 lakh crore; net ₹6.65 lakh crore
Gross ₹17.20 lakh crore; net ₹11.73 lakh crore
Gross ₹16.96 lakh crore; net ₹17.20 lakh crore
103.x: Gross market borrowing through dated securities was ₹17.20 lakh crore and net market borrowing was ₹11.73 lakh crore in 2026-27.
103.tq: Watch for reversal of gross and net figures.
103.sec: Market borrowings - share in capital receipts; household savings and government borrowing  [APPSC]

103.s:
Consider the following statements regarding market borrowing in 2026-27:

2. The weighted average yield was 6.65%.
3. Switches and buybacks were undertaken to ease redemption pressures.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
103.x: All three statements are correct. The weighted average maturity was 19.03 years, the yield was 6.65%, and switches and buybacks were used to ease redemptions.
103.tq: Combine two numerical facts with the associated debt-management measure.
103.sec: Market borrowings - share in capital receipts; household savings and government borrowing  [APPSC]

103.s: The total borrowing requirement of the Union Government for 2026-27 was estimated at:
103.x: The total borrowing requirement for 2026-27 was estimated at ₹16,95,768 crore.

103.sec: Market borrowings - share in capital receipts; household savings and government borrowing  [APPSC]

103.s:
Household financial savings contribute to government borrowing through which of the following channels?
1. Bank deposits reflected through SLR holdings
2. Small savings and the National Small Savings Fund
3. Insurance and provident funds
4. Only direct purchase of foreign sovereign bonds
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
103.x: Household savings flow to government borrowing through bank deposits, small savings/NSSF, and insurance and provident funds. Direct purchase of foreign sovereign bonds is not the stated channel.
103.tq: Find the single over-exclusive or unrelated channel among several genuine domestic channels.
103.sec: Market borrowings - share in capital receipts; household savings and government borrowing  [APPSC]

103.s:
Consider the following statements regarding State borrowing:
1. A State owing any amount to the Centre requires the Centre's consent to borrow further.
2. Since 2005-06, external loans to States have been routed through the Centre.
3. For general category States, such external loans are provided on a back-to-back basis.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
103.x: All three statements are correct under the stated framework for State borrowing and external loans.
103.tq: Test the constitutional consent rule together with the post-2005-06 borrowing arrangement.
103.sec: State borrowing - net borrowing ceiling, highest debt-GSDP States, AP liabilities  [APPSC]

103.s: The net borrowing ceiling for States for 2021-22, as recommended by the Fifteenth Finance Commission, was:

103.sec: State borrowing - net borrowing ceiling, highest debt-GSDP States, AP liabilities  [APPSC]

103.s: The Sixteenth Finance Commission has capped the fiscal deficit of States at what percentage of GSDP for 2026-31?
103.x: The fiscal deficit of States has been capped at 3% of GSDP for 2026-31 under the Sixteenth Finance Commission framework.
103.tq: Discriminate between the 2021-22 borrowing ceiling and the 2026-31 fiscal-deficit cap.
103.sec: State borrowing - net borrowing ceiling, highest debt-GSDP States, AP liabilities  [APPSC]

103.s: Which State had the highest debt or outstanding liabilities as a percentage of GSDP among the following in 2023-24?
103.x: Punjab had the highest ratio among the listed States at 42.9% of GSDP in 2023-24, followed by West Bengal at 38.3%, Rajasthan at 37.9% and Andhra Pradesh at 34.6%.

B. Andhra Pradesh
C. Punjab
D. West Bengal

103.tq: Rank the figures from highest to lowest before checking the sequence options.
103.sec: State borrowing - net borrowing ceiling, highest debt-GSDP States, AP liabilities  [APPSC]

103.s: Which of the following correctly describes Andhra Pradesh's debt position in 2025-26 revised estimates?

Total debt ₹7,11,094 crore and 36.04% of GSDP

Total debt ₹6,35,177 crore and 36.04% of GSDP

103.tq: Match the amount with the correct year and estimate category.
103.sec: State borrowing - net borrowing ceiling, highest debt-GSDP States, AP liabilities  [APPSC]

103.s: Which one of the following statements regarding Andhra Pradesh's debt is NOT correct?
o: Market borrowing accounted for only 12% of Andhra Pradesh's debt in 2023-24 revised estimates.
Interest payments were ₹37,233 crore in 2025-26 revised estimates.
Market borrowing was ₹4,83,093 crore in 2025-26 revised estimates.
Market borrowing is the largest component of the State's debt.
103.x: Market borrowing accounted for 75% of Andhra Pradesh's debt in 2023-24 RE, not 12%. The 12% share related to other liabilities in the composition table.

103.sec: State borrowing - net borrowing ceiling, highest debt-GSDP States, AP liabilities  [APPSC]

103.s: According to the 2023-24 revised estimates, the correct descending order of components of Andhra Pradesh's debt is:
o: Market loans > central loans ≈ provident funds > others > small savings
Others > market loans > provident funds > central loans > small savings
Small savings > provident funds > central loans > others > market loans
Market loans > others > central loans ≈ provident funds > small savings

103.tq: Arrange components by percentage and preserve the approximate tie.
103.sec: State borrowing - net borrowing ceiling, highest debt-GSDP States, AP liabilities  [APPSC]

103.s: Which one of the following correctly states Andhra Pradesh's Budget Estimate for outstanding liabilities in 2026-27?

103.s:
Which of the following statements regarding State finances is correct?
1. States borrowed ₹5.23 trillion up to October 2025.
2. This represented 62% of the FY26 borrowing plan.
3. The combined fiscal deficit of States was 3.2% of GDP in FY25.
4. Eighteen States recorded fiscal deficits above 3% in FY24.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
103.x: All four statements are correct: States borrowed ₹5.23 trillion by October 2025, equal to 62% of the FY26 plan; the combined FY25 deficit was 3.2% of GDP; and 18 States exceeded 3% in FY24.
103.tq: Check each time-bound fiscal statistic separately before selecting the coded combination.
103.sec: State borrowing - net borrowing ceiling, highest debt-GSDP States, AP liabilities  [APPSC]

103.s: India's external debt at the end of December 2024 was estimated at:
o: USD 635.177 billion, equivalent to 36.04% of GDP
USD 711.82 billion, equivalent to 18.4% of GDP
USD 718.2 billion, equivalent to 20.4% of GDP
USD 718.2 billion, equivalent to 18.4% of GDP
103.x: India's external debt stood at USD 718.2 billion at end-December 2024, equivalent to 18.4% of GDP in the cited estimate.
103.tq: Keep the external-debt amount and its GDP ratio together while rejecting figures from other debt categories.
103.sec: External debt - composition, sovereign share, currency, publisher  [other exams]

103.s:
Consider the following statements about India's external debt:
1. Its external debt-to-GDP ratio was reported as 20.4% in the RBI-based estimate.
2. Foreign exchange reserves covered 90% of external debt.
3. India ranked 21st in the world and 11th among G20 countries.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
103.x: All three statements are correct for the cited RBI and Economic Survey-based indicators.
103.tq: Combine ratio, reserve-cover and ranking data without confusing alternative estimates.
103.sec: External debt - composition, sovereign share, currency, publisher  [other exams]

103.s: Historically, the largest component of India's external debt has been:
103.x: Commercial borrowings have historically been the largest component of India's external debt.
103.tq: Identify the principal historical component while excluding domestic-liability categories.
103.sec: External debt - composition, sovereign share, currency, publisher  [other exams]

103.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched with India's sovereign external borrowing?
o: Primarily multilateral, concessional and project-linked — ADB is the largest multilateral lender
Primarily commercial and non-concessional — ADB is excluded
Primarily domestic and short-term — NDB is the sole lender
Primarily denominated in domestic currency — AIIB is the only lender
103.x: Sovereign external borrowing is mostly multilateral, concessional and project-linked. The ADB is the largest multilateral lender, with a 32.8% share, followed by institutions including the World Bank, NDB and AIIB.
103.tq: Match the borrowing character with the correct multilateral lender and avoid absolute distractors.
103.sec: External debt - composition, sovereign share, currency, publisher  [other exams]

103.s: Which institution publishes ‘India's External Debt: A Status Report’?
o: Department of Economic Affairs, Ministry of Finance
103.x: The report is published by the Department of Economic Affairs under the Ministry of Finance. The RBI compiles the quarterly external-debt data.
103.tq: Distinguish the institution that publishes the report from the institution that compiles quarterly data.
103.sec: External debt - composition, sovereign share, currency, publisher  [other exams]

103.s: The term ‘debt trap’ refers to a situation in which the government:
o: borrows to repay the principal of external debt
borrows to pay interest on past debt
uses surplus revenue to retire public debt
103.x: A debt trap occurs when fresh borrowing is used to meet interest obligations on past debt.
103.tq: Use the exact meaning of the paired fiscal terms.
103.sec: Debt sustainability - debt trap, interest-growth differential, primary balance  [other exams]

103.s: With reference to the primary deficit, which one of the following statements is correct?
o: A primary deficit necessarily indicates that the debt-GDP ratio is falling.
A zero primary deficit means fresh borrowing covers only interest payments.
A primary deficit is equal to the fiscal deficit plus interest payments.
A zero primary deficit means there is no outstanding public debt.
103.x: A zero primary deficit means that, after excluding interest payments, the government does not need additional borrowing; fresh borrowing is only for interest.
103.tq: Split the fiscal-deficit and primary-deficit meanings.
103.sec: Debt sustainability - debt trap, interest-growth differential, primary balance  [other exams]

103.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the interest-growth differential:
1. If nominal GDP growth exceeds the effective interest rate, the debt-GDP ratio can decline even with a small primary deficit.
2. A primary surplus is needed when the effective interest rate exceeds nominal GDP growth.
3. The relevant differential is represented as r − g, where r is the effective interest rate and g is nominal GDP growth.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
103.x: All three statements correctly describe the interest-growth differential and its implications for debt sustainability.
103.tq: Check the direction of r and g before selecting the coded combination.
103.sec: Debt sustainability - debt trap, interest-growth differential, primary balance  [other exams]

103.s: For 2026-27, which one of the following correctly represents the effective interest rate on Central debt and nominal GDP growth?

103.tq: Match the two figures without reversing their order.
103.sec: Debt sustainability - debt trap, interest-growth differential, primary balance  [other exams]

103.s: The effective interest rate on Central debt in 2026-27 was stated to have been rising for:
103.x: The effective interest rate on Central debt, placed at 7.12% for 2026-27, had been rising for three years.
103.tq: Distinguish the duration attached to a current fiscal figure.
103.sec: Debt sustainability - debt trap, interest-growth differential, primary balance  [other exams]

103.s: Interest payments on Central debt are approximately what proportion of revenue receipts?
103.x: Interest payments account for about 40% of revenue receipts, thereby limiting the fiscal space for other expenditure.
103.tq: Use the closest exact share rather than an approximate distractor.
103.sec: Debt sustainability - debt trap, interest-growth differential, primary balance  [other exams]

103.s: Which of the following factors is associated with the assessment that India’s debt risks are low?
o: A very high share of floating-rate debt
A small, long-term and concessional external debt
Absence of interest payments on public debt
Exclusive dependence on short-term external borrowing
103.x: India’s external debt is described as small, long-term and concessional. Floating-rate debt was only 4.1% at the end of FY24.
103.tq: Identify the positive debt-risk characteristics and reject extreme claims.
103.sec: Debt sustainability - debt trap, interest-growth differential, primary balance  [other exams]

103.tq: Test the precise percentage from the debt-risk assessment.
103.sec: Debt sustainability - debt trap, interest-growth differential, primary balance  [other exams]

103.s: Which pair of indicators is especially relevant for assessing the debt sustainability of States?
o: Debt-GSDP ratio and interest payments-to-revenue receipts ratio
Current account deficit and foreign exchange reserves
Fiscal deficit-to-GDP ratio and export-import ratio
103.x: For States, debt-GSDP and interest payments as a proportion of revenue receipts are the key sustainability ratios.
103.tq: Match the level of government with its relevant sustainability indicators.
103.sec: Debt sustainability - debt trap, interest-growth differential, primary balance  [other exams]

103.s: According to the Budget estimates for 2026-27, the Centre’s debt-GDP ratio is:
103.x: The Centre’s debt-GDP ratio is estimated at 55.6% in BE 2026-27. The revised estimate for 2025-26 is 56.1%.

103.tq: Compare budget estimate, revised estimate and peak-year values.
103.sec: General government debt-GDP - Centre, States, combined; targets  [other exams]

103.sec: General government debt-GDP - Centre, States, combined; targets  [other exams]

103.sec: General government debt-GDP - Centre, States, combined; targets  [other exams]

103.sec: General government debt-GDP - Centre, States, combined; targets  [other exams]

103.s: Which change was made in Budget 2026-27 regarding the principal fiscal anchor?
o: Revenue deficit replaced the primary balance.
The current account deficit replaced public debt.
The fiscal deficit replaced the debt-GDP ratio.
The debt-GDP ratio replaced the fiscal deficit.
103.x: Budget 2026-27 made the debt-GDP ratio the primary target instead of the fiscal deficit.
103.tq: Test the policy shift by identifying what replaced what.
103.sec: General government debt-GDP - Centre, States, combined; targets  [other exams]

103.s: Which of the following best describes off-budget borrowing?
o: Borrowing by private firms that is guaranteed by foreign banks
Borrowing by the RBI exclusively for monetary operations
Borrowing by households that is recorded under capital receipts
Loans raised by government-owned entities and serviced from the budget without appearing in the deficit
103.x: Off-budget borrowing is raised by PSUs, SPVs or other government-owned entities but serviced from the government budget, so it does not appear directly in the deficit.
103.tq: Apply the definition to the borrower, servicing source and accounting treatment.

103.s: The classic Central government example of off-budget borrowing involved the FCI borrowing from the NSSF to:
103.x: The Food Corporation of India borrowed from the National Small Savings Fund to cover unpaid food subsidy obligations.

103.sec: Off-budget borrowing - FCI and NSSF, SPVs, guarantees, AP corporations

103.s: What was the effect of Budget 2021-22 on the FCI-NSSF food subsidy arrangement?
o: It converted the subsidy into an external loan.
It expanded the arrangement and shifted the subsidy off-budget.
It transferred the subsidy to State governments.
It ended the arrangement and placed the food subsidy fully on-budget.
103.x: Budget 2021-22 ended the FCI borrowing arrangement with the NSSF and placed the food subsidy fully on-budget.
103.tq: Test the policy reversal rather than the original borrowing mechanism.
103.sec: Off-budget borrowing - FCI and NSSF, SPVs, guarantees, AP corporations

103.s: Under the FRBM framework, new Central government guarantees are limited to what proportion of GDP in a year?
103.x: The FRBM limit for new Central government guarantees is 0.5% of GDP in a year.

103.sec: Off-budget borrowing - FCI and NSSF, SPVs, guarantees, AP corporations

103.s: Government guarantees are treated as:

₹1.77 lakh crore, equal to 9.7% of GSDP

103.sec: Off-budget borrowing - FCI and NSSF, SPVs, guarantees, AP corporations

103.s: Which one of the following correctly states the reported off-budget debt of Andhra Pradesh as of 31 March 2024?
103.x: The reported off-budget debt of Andhra Pradesh was ₹1,40,470 crore as of 31 March 2024.

103.s:
Consider the following statements about Andhra Pradesh’s liabilities:
1. Guarantees amounted to ₹1,77,328 crore, or 10% of GSDP.

103.sec: Off-budget borrowing - FCI and NSSF, SPVs, guarantees, AP corporations

o: Permit unlimited borrowing through State corporations
Exclude guarantees from all debt calculations
Stop off-budget borrowing and bring existing debt on-budget
Transfer all off-budget debt to the RBI

103.s: Which one of the following was NOT part of the 16th Finance Commission’s recommendation on off-budget borrowing?
o: Widen the definitions of deficit and debt
103.x: The recommendation was to stop and disclose such borrowing more fully, not to permit it without disclosure.
103.tq: Find the option that reverses the stated reform recommendation.
103.sec: Off-budget borrowing - FCI and NSSF, SPVs, guarantees, AP corporations

103.s: Which institution manages the public debt of the Centre and the States and also acts as banker to them under the RBI Act, 1934?
o: Securities and Exchange Board of India
103.x: The Reserve Bank of India manages public debt and acts as banker to the Central and State governments under the RBI Act, 1934.

103.s: The Public Debt Office of the RBI is responsible for:
o: auditing the accounts of State governments
approving all foreign direct investment proposals
fixing GST rates and administering customs duty
issuing, servicing and maintaining records of government securities
103.x: The RBI’s Public Debt Office handles the issue, servicing and records of government securities.

Public Debt Office of the RBI

o: issues both currency and corporate bonds
regulates both insurance and pension funds
audits both Central and State budgets
conducts monetary policy while also managing public debt

103.s:
Consider the following statements about the Public Debt Management Cell:
1. It was set up in 2016 in the Department of Economic Affairs.
2. It is headed by the Joint Secretary (Budget).
3. It was intended as a transition to an independent statutory PDMA.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
103.x: The PDMC was established in 2016 in the DEA, headed by the Joint Secretary (Budget), as a transitional arrangement for a statutory PDMA.

It has not yet been created as an independent statutory agency.
It replaced the RBI’s Public Debt Office immediately.
It functions under SEBI as the regulator of government securities.

103.tq: Distinguish a proposal and transitional mechanism from an actually established body.

103.s: Which one of the following best explains why public debt has become a fiscal anchor?
o: A debt ratio has no relationship with revenue receipts.
Debt determines only the quantity of currency in circulation.
Debt is excluded from sovereign-rating assessments.
High interest payments can squeeze expenditure on other public purposes.

Its debt stock has stopped growing because off-budget borrowing is prohibited.

Its debt-to-GSDP ratio is fixed at 20% by the FRBM Act.
103.x: Andhra Pradesh’s debt-to-GSDP ratio is described as stabilising in the mid-30s, while the absolute debt stock continues to increase.
103.tq: Distinguish a stabilising ratio from a declining absolute debt stock.
103.sec: Universal angles

103.s: After Q1 of 2026-27, the Centre’s debt-GDP ratio on the new GDP series was estimated at:
103.x: The Centre’s debt-GDP ratio was estimated at 55.8% after Q1 2026-27 on the new GDP series.
103.tq: Test the current estimate against nearby historical and target values.
103.sec: Universal angles

103.s: Which concern is associated with State off-budget borrowings and guarantees?
o: They are excluded from all contingent-liability calculations by law.
They automatically reduce the interest burden on the government.
They improve the sovereign rating by shifting debt to PSUs.
They make consolidated public debt appear lower than it actually is and may weigh on sovereign ratings.
103.x: State off-budget borrowings and guarantees can conceal the true consolidated debt burden and adversely affect perceptions of sovereign creditworthiness.
103.tq: Trace the effect of hidden liabilities on consolidated debt and ratings.
103.sec: Universal angles

103.s: According to the Budget Estimates for 2026-27, Andhra Pradesh’s debt is expected to cross:
103.x: Andhra Pradesh’s debt is projected to cross ₹7 lakh crore in BE 2026-27.
103.tq: Identify the threshold figure attached to the State budget estimate.
103.sec: Universal angles

105.s: Which one of the following correctly represents the Revenue Deficit of the Government?
o: Total expenditure minus total receipts including borrowings
105.x: Revenue Deficit is calculated as revenue expenditure minus revenue receipts. It indicates borrowing for day-to-day consumption or dissaving.
105.tq: Use the exact formula and distinguish revenue deficit from fiscal and primary deficits.
105.sec: Deficit definitions - formulas and calculation from budget figures  [APPSC]

105.s: Effective Revenue Deficit is calculated as:
o: Revenue deficit minus grants for creation of capital assets
Revenue deficit plus grants for creation of capital assets
105.x: Effective Revenue Deficit equals Revenue Deficit minus grants for creation of capital assets. Such grants are excluded from the consumption component because they help create assets.
105.tq: Split the formula into the basic deficit and the qualifying deduction.
105.sec: Deficit definitions - formulas and calculation from budget figures  [APPSC]

105.s: Fiscal Deficit is defined as:
o: Total receipts including borrowings minus total expenditure
Total expenditure minus total receipts excluding borrowings
105.x: Fiscal Deficit is total expenditure minus total receipts excluding borrowings. It represents the total borrowing requirement of the government.
105.tq: Distinguish receipts excluding borrowings from total receipts including borrowings.
105.sec: Deficit definitions - formulas and calculation from budget figures  [APPSC]

105.s:
Consider the following statements regarding fiscal and revenue deficits:
1. Fiscal Deficit shows the total borrowing requirement of the government from all sources.
2. Revenue Deficit indicates borrowing for day-to-day consumption.
3. Fiscal Deficit is always equal to Revenue Deficit.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
105.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because fiscal deficit also includes the capital account components and is not necessarily equal to revenue deficit.
105.tq: Find the one overgeneralised comparison and retain the two definition-based statements.
105.sec: Deficit definitions - formulas and calculation from budget figures  [APPSC]

105.s: Gross Fiscal Deficit differs from Net Fiscal Deficit because Net Fiscal Deficit:
o: subtracts the Centre's net lending from Gross Fiscal Deficit
105.x: Gross Fiscal Deficit is the fiscal deficit before deducting the Centre's net lending. Net Fiscal Deficit is obtained by subtracting such net lending from the gross figure.
105.tq: Focus on the precise item removed in a gross-versus-net comparison.
105.sec: Deficit definitions - formulas and calculation from budget figures  [APPSC]

105.s: The term ‘Monetised Deficit’ refers to:
o: The portion of revenue deficit covered by grants
The portion of deficit financed through external commercial borrowing
The portion of deficit financed by borrowing from the public
The portion of deficit financed by the Reserve Bank of India through creation of high-powered money
105.x: Monetised Deficit is the part of the deficit financed by the RBI, involving an increase in RBI credit to the government and creation of high-powered money.
105.tq: Match the specialised deficit term with its financing source and monetary effect.
105.sec: Deficit definitions - formulas and calculation from budget figures  [APPSC]

105.s: A government has revenue receipts of ₹3,00,000 crore and revenue expenditure of ₹3,50,000 crore. Its Revenue Deficit is:
105.x: Revenue Deficit = Revenue Expenditure − Revenue Receipts = ₹3,50,000 crore − ₹3,00,000 crore = ₹50,000 crore.
105.tq: Apply the revenue-deficit formula directly to the two revenue-account figures.
105.sec: Deficit definitions - formulas and calculation from budget figures  [APPSC]

105.s: In the budget figures where Fiscal Deficit is ₹1,50,000 crore and interest payments are ₹1,20,000 crore, the Primary Deficit is:
105.x: Primary Deficit = Fiscal Deficit − Interest Payments = ₹1,50,000 crore − ₹1,20,000 crore = ₹30,000 crore.
105.tq: Use the primary-deficit formula after identifying the two supplied figures.
105.sec: Deficit definitions - formulas and calculation from budget figures  [APPSC]

105.s: If the Fiscal Deficit is ₹4 crore and GDP is ₹400 crore, the Fiscal Deficit as a percentage of GDP will be:
105.x: Fiscal Deficit as a percentage of GDP = (₹4 crore ÷ ₹400 crore) × 100 = 1 percent.
105.tq: Convert the deficit-to-GDP ratio into a percentage by multiplying by 100.
105.sec: Deficit definitions - formulas and calculation from budget figures  [APPSC]

105.s:
Arrange the following developments in chronological order:
A. FRBM amendment incorporating Effective Revenue Deficit
B. Agreement between the RBI and Government relating to ad hoc Treasury Bills
C. Abolition of ad hoc Treasury Bills
D. Introduction of Effective Revenue Deficit in the Union Budget
105.x: The correct sequence is the 1994 agreement, abolition of ad hoc Treasury Bills from 1 April 1997, introduction of ERD in 2011-12, and its incorporation through the 2012 amendment.
105.tq: Fix the dated anchor points first and then place the budget and amendment developments.
105.sec: Deficit definitions - formulas and calculation from budget figures  [APPSC]

105.s: Which one of the following statements regarding the old concept of Budget Deficit is NOT correct?
o: It included revenue and capital receipts in total receipts.
It was calculated as total expenditure minus total receipts including borrowings.
It is calculated as fiscal deficit minus interest payments.
It was used when ad hoc Treasury Bills financed the gap.
105.x: Fiscal Deficit minus interest payments gives Primary Deficit, not Budget Deficit. Budget Deficit was the difference between total expenditure and total receipts including borrowings.
105.tq: Eliminate the statement that gives the formula of another deficit concept.
105.sec: Deficit definitions - formulas and calculation from budget figures  [APPSC]

105.s: Budget Deficit ceased to be the headline measure after:
o: The introduction of Effective Revenue Deficit in 2011-12
The abolition of ad hoc Treasury Bills in 1997
The introduction of Ways and Means Advances in 1997
105.x: Budget Deficit stopped being the headline measure after ad hoc Treasury Bills were abolished in 1997. The gap was thereafter considered through other deficit measures and financing arrangements.
105.tq: Link the change in the headline indicator to the institutional financing reform that caused it.
105.sec: Deficit definitions - formulas and calculation from budget figures  [APPSC]

105.s: In Indian public finance, deficit financing primarily means covering a government financing gap by:
o: Drawing down cash balances, borrowing from the RBI or issuing new currency
Transferring revenue receipts to the central bank
105.x: Deficit financing in the Indian context includes drawing down cash balances, borrowing from the RBI and issuing new currency to cover the financing gap.
105.tq: Identify the combination of recognised financing methods rather than an individual fiscal measure.
105.sec: Deficit financing - meaning, sources, money supply, ad hoc T-Bills, WMA  [APPSC]

105.s:
Consider the following statements about the effects of deficit financing:
1. RBI money creation tends to increase money supply and inflation.
2. Borrowing from the public absorbs liquidity and may slow private economic activity.
3. External borrowing may create currency risk.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
105.x: All three statements are correct. RBI financing creates money, public borrowing absorbs liquidity, and external borrowing exposes the government or economy to currency risk.
105.tq: Test the different channels of deficit financing separately before selecting the combined code.
105.sec: Deficit financing - meaning, sources, money supply, ad hoc T-Bills, WMA  [APPSC]

105.s: Ad hoc Treasury Bills were associated with:
o: Long-term borrowing exclusively from foreign governments
Temporary advances to State Governments for cash mismatches
Automatic monetisation of the Centre's deficit by the RBI
Collection of indirect taxes by the RBI
105.x: Ad hoc Treasury Bills enabled automatic monetisation of the Centre's deficit by the RBI. They were later abolished and replaced by Ways and Means Advances.
105.tq: Distinguish automatic deficit monetisation from temporary cash-management advances.
105.sec: Deficit financing - meaning, sources, money supply, ad hoc T-Bills, WMA  [APPSC]

105.s: Ad hoc Treasury Bills were abolished with effect from:
105.x: Ad hoc Treasury Bills were abolished from 1 April 1997. The reform followed the 1994 agreement between the RBI and the Government and they were replaced by WMA.
105.tq: Use the exact effective date rather than the year of the preceding agreement.
105.sec: Deficit financing - meaning, sources, money supply, ad hoc T-Bills, WMA  [APPSC]

105.s: Ways and Means Advances are intended to provide:
o: Temporary RBI advances to meet day-to-day cash mismatches of the Centre and States
Automatic monetisation of all government expenditure
105.x: WMA are temporary advances provided by the RBI to the Centre and States to meet day-to-day cash mismatches. They are not a permanent source of deficit financing.
105.tq: Apply the cash-management purpose of WMA to distinguish it from permanent borrowing.
105.sec: Deficit financing - meaning, sources, money supply, ad hoc T-Bills, WMA  [APPSC]

105.s: When government borrowing from the RBI under Ways and Means Advances exceeds the prescribed limit, it is treated as:
105.x: Use of WMA beyond the prescribed limit is treated as an overdraft. WMA themselves are intended for temporary cash mismatches.
105.tq: Discriminate between the normal temporary facility and the status created when its limit is exceeded.
105.sec: Deficit financing - meaning, sources, money supply, ad hoc T-Bills, WMA

105.s: With effect from 2006-07, the RBI was generally barred from:
o: Purchasing government securities in the secondary market
Subscribing to primary issues of Government securities
Providing Ways and Means Advances to State Governments
105.x: From 2006-07, the RBI was barred from subscribing to primary issues of Government securities, except under the escape clause. This restriction limits routine monetisation of the deficit.
105.tq: Identify the specific primary-market restriction and do not confuse it with cash management or secondary-market operations.
105.sec: Deficit financing - meaning, sources, money supply, ad hoc T-Bills, WMA

105.s: Which one of the following is the correct qualification to the restriction on RBI subscription to primary issues of Government securities?
o: It applies only during a revenue surplus.
It has no exceptions under any circumstances.
It may be relaxed under the escape clause.
It applies only to State Government securities.
105.x: The restriction applies under normal conditions, but subscription may be permitted under the escape clause. The rule is not an absolute prohibition in every circumstance.
105.tq: Look for the exception clause instead of accepting an absolute statement about a statutory restriction.
105.sec: Deficit financing - meaning, sources, money supply, ad hoc T-Bills, WMA

105.s: Which one of the following correctly expresses the relationship between Fiscal Deficit (FD) and Primary Deficit (PD), when interest payments are positive?
o: FD and PD are always equal
There is no definite relationship between FD and PD
FD is always greater than PD
PD is always greater than FD
105.x: Primary Deficit is calculated as Fiscal Deficit minus interest payments. Therefore, when interest payments are positive, Fiscal Deficit is greater than Primary Deficit.
105.tq: Use the formula and check the effect of positive interest payments.
105.sec: Relationship between deficits - which is larger, zero primary deficit  [APPSC]

105.s: Fiscal Deficit is greater than Revenue Deficit when which of the following conditions is satisfied?
o: Capital expenditure exceeds non-debt capital receipts
105.x: Fiscal Deficit exceeds Revenue Deficit when capital expenditure is greater than non-debt capital receipts. The difference reflects the financing requirement beyond the revenue account.
105.tq: Split the deficit definitions into revenue and capital components.
105.sec: Relationship between deficits - which is larger, zero primary deficit  [APPSC]

105.s: Which one of the following relationships between Effective Revenue Deficit (ERD) and Revenue Deficit (RD) is correct?
o: ERD is always greater than RD
ERD has no relationship with RD
ERD is equal to RD only when interest payments are positive
ERD is less than or equal to RD
105.x: Effective Revenue Deficit is obtained after deducting grants for creation of capital assets from Revenue Deficit. Hence, ERD is less than or equal to RD.
105.tq: Identify the deduction used to derive the narrower deficit measure.
105.sec: Relationship between deficits - which is larger, zero primary deficit  [APPSC]

105.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the deficit estimates for 2026–27 (Budget Estimates):
1. Fiscal Deficit is estimated at 4.3 per cent of GDP.
2. Revenue Deficit is estimated at 1.5 per cent of GDP.
3. Primary Deficit is estimated at 0.7 per cent of GDP.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
105.x: The estimates are Fiscal Deficit 4.3 per cent, Revenue Deficit 1.5 per cent and Primary Deficit 0.7 per cent of GDP. Thus, all three statements are correct.
105.tq: Verify each numerical statement independently before selecting the code.
105.sec: Relationship between deficits - which is larger, zero primary deficit  [APPSC]

105.s: A zero Primary Deficit indicates that the government is borrowing mainly to:
105.x: Primary Deficit equals Fiscal Deficit minus interest payments. When it is zero, borrowing is equal to interest payments and is being used only to service past debt.
105.tq: Translate a zero value in the deficit formula into its fiscal meaning.
105.sec: Relationship between deficits - which is larger, zero primary deficit  [APPSC]

105.s: A zero Primary Deficit is generally regarded as a warning signal of a debt trap because it implies that:
o: Borrowing is being used to make interest payments
Non-interest expenditure is fully financed by tax revenue
Capital receipts are greater than total expenditure
105.x: With zero Primary Deficit, the government borrows an amount equal to its interest payments. Borrowing to pay interest on earlier loans is a characteristic warning sign of a debt trap.
105.tq: Recognise the debt-service implication of a zero primary balance.
105.sec: Relationship between deficits - which is larger, zero primary deficit  [APPSC]

105.s: What does a zero Revenue Deficit signify?
o: Zero Fiscal Deficit in every year
105.x: Zero Revenue Deficit means that revenue receipts are equal to revenue expenditure. It represents a balanced revenue budget, though it does not necessarily imply zero Fiscal Deficit.
105.tq: Distinguish the revenue account from the overall budget.
105.sec: Relationship between deficits - which is larger, zero primary deficit  [APPSC]

105.s: A large share of Revenue Deficit in Fiscal Deficit indicates that borrowing is substantially being used for:
105.x: When Revenue Deficit forms a large part of Fiscal Deficit, borrowing is financing revenue expenditure or consumption rather than productive capital formation.
105.tq: Interpret the composition of a deficit rather than its size alone.
105.sec: Relationship between deficits - which is larger, zero primary deficit  [APPSC]

105.s: A Primary Surplus, represented by a negative Primary Deficit, means that:
o: Revenue receipts are lower than revenue expenditure
Fiscal Deficit is greater than Revenue Deficit
Non-interest expenditure is fully covered by non-debt receipts
Interest payments are greater than total expenditure
105.x: A Primary Surplus occurs when non-debt receipts cover non-interest expenditure completely and leave an excess. It is expressed as a negative Primary Deficit.
105.tq: Use the sign convention to identify the meaning of a negative deficit.
105.sec: Relationship between deficits - which is larger, zero primary deficit  [APPSC]

105.s: Fiscal policy refers primarily to the use of government revenue and expenditure to influence:
105.x: Fiscal policy uses government revenue and expenditure to influence aggregate demand, resource allocation and income distribution.
105.tq: Select the option covering the full scope of the policy definition.
105.sec: Fiscal policy - definition, instruments vs monetary policy  [APPSC]

105.s:
Which of the following are instruments of fiscal policy?
1. Taxation
2. Public expenditure
3. Public borrowing
4. Subsidies and Direct Benefit Transfers
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
105.x: Taxation, public expenditure, public borrowing, subsidies and Direct Benefit Transfers are fiscal policy instruments. Public investment through PLI is also included among fiscal instruments.
105.tq: Test the complete list of instruments rather than identifying only the familiar ones.
105.sec: Fiscal policy - definition, instruments vs monetary policy  [APPSC]

105.s: Which authority is primarily responsible for monetary policy in India?
o: RBI and the Monetary Policy Committee
105.x: Monetary policy is conducted by the Reserve Bank of India through the Monetary Policy Committee. Fiscal policy is made by the government, with legislative backing.
105.tq: Apply the ‘who would do this job?’ approach to policy authority questions.
105.sec: Fiscal policy - definition, instruments vs monetary policy  [APPSC]

105.s: Which of the following is a monetary policy instrument rather than a fiscal policy instrument?
105.x: The repo rate is a monetary policy instrument used by the RBI and the MPC. Public expenditure, subsidies and public borrowing are fiscal instruments.
105.tq: Discriminate between closely related fiscal and monetary instruments.
105.sec: Fiscal policy - definition, instruments vs monetary policy  [APPSC]

105.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Fiscal policy generally operates through a budget cycle and is relatively slow.
2. Monetary policy can operate relatively quickly through the bi-monthly decisions of the MPC.
3. Fiscal policy usually has a direct and targeted impact, whereas monetary policy works indirectly through credit.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
105.x: Fiscal policy is slower because it generally works through the budget cycle and has direct, targeted effects. Monetary policy can act faster through the bi-monthly MPC process and affects the economy indirectly through credit.
105.tq: Compare all corresponding rows of the policy comparison.
105.sec: Fiscal policy - definition, instruments vs monetary policy  [APPSC]

105.s: The word ‘fiscal’ is derived from the Latin term ‘fiscus’, which means:
105.x: The term fiscal is derived from the Latin word fiscus, meaning a basket or public purse. It is associated with government revenue and expenditure.
105.tq: Test an exact terminology-based fact without confusing it with a policy instrument.
105.sec: Fiscal policy - definition, instruments vs monetary policy  [APPSC]

105.s: Which department prepares the Union Budget, formally presented as the Annual Financial Statement under Article 112 of the Constitution?
105.x: The Department of Economic Affairs prepares the Union Budget. The Annual Financial Statement is referred to in Article 112 of the Constitution.
105.tq: Match the constitutional document with the responsible department.
105.sec: Fiscal policy - definition, instruments vs monetary policy  [APPSC]

105.s: Which one of the following statements is correct regarding the term ‘Budget’ in the Constitution of India?
o: The word Budget does not appear in the Constitution; Article 112 refers to the Annual Financial Statement
The term Budget appears in the Constitution but not in the Annual Financial Statement
The Constitution uses Budget and Annual Financial Statement as identical expressions
The Constitution defines the term Budget in Article 112
105.x: The Constitution does not use the word ‘Budget’. Article 112 refers to the Annual Financial Statement, which is popularly presented as the Union Budget.
105.tq: Watch for the exact official constitutional expression rather than the commonly used name.
105.sec: Fiscal policy - definition, instruments vs monetary policy  [APPSC]

105.s: Public borrowing used to finance the Fiscal Deficit may be classified as:
o: Only external borrowing through multilateral institutions
105.x: Public borrowing may be internal, such as bonds, Treasury Bills and small savings, or external, such as multilateral borrowing and sovereign bonds. It finances the Fiscal Deficit.
105.tq: Identify the complete classification and reject the ‘only’ alternatives.
105.sec: Fiscal policy - definition, instruments vs monetary policy  [APPSC]

105.s: Which of the following functions of the budget was identified by Richard Musgrave as involving the provision of public goods and allocation of resources?
105.x: The allocation function provides public goods and allocates resources. Musgrave identified allocation, distribution and stabilisation as the three principal budget functions.
105.tq: Link each function with its distinctive meaning.
105.sec: Fiscal policy objectives - allocation, distribution, stabilisation (Musgrave)  [APPSC]

105.s: Progressive taxation and welfare spending primarily serve which fiscal function?
105.x: The distribution function seeks to reduce inequality through progressive taxation and welfare spending, thereby changing the distribution of disposable income.
105.tq: Infer the fiscal function from the stated policy instrument and objective.
105.sec: Fiscal policy objectives - allocation, distribution, stabilisation (Musgrave)  [APPSC]

105.s: The stabilisation function of fiscal policy is mainly concerned with:
o: Smoothing economic cycles and controlling inflation and unemployment
105.x: The stabilisation function seeks to smooth the business cycle and address inflation and unemployment through appropriate fiscal action.
105.tq: Choose the option that combines the cycle, inflation and employment dimensions.
105.sec: Fiscal policy objectives - allocation, distribution, stabilisation (Musgrave)  [APPSC]

105.s:
Consider the following statements about Richard Musgrave:
1. He identified allocation, distribution and stabilisation as three budget functions.
2. He popularised the term fiscal federalism in 1959.
3. He restricted the role of fiscal policy exclusively to economic growth.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
105.x: Musgrave identified the three budget functions and popularised the term fiscal federalism in 1959. His framework was not restricted exclusively to economic growth.
